Evidence • src/agents/insights/agent.py#InsightsAgent.run — Uses InsightsOutput schema • src/llm/structured.py#validate_structured_output — Validation logic

Consequences

Benefits • Reliable parsing • Type checking • Clear interface

Costs • Prompt overhead • LLM may struggle with complex schemas

Failure modes • Validation errors if LLM deviates

Reuse notes • Define Pydantic models for all agent outputs. • Keep schemas as simple as possible to reduce validation failures.

Confidence

High — the agent and validation logic are directly evidenced via schema usage and a dedicated validation function.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: Standardize distributed OpenTelemetry tracing and structured metric envelopes across autonomous agent execution workflows to trace invocation latency, token spend, and step failure boundaries transparently.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: In multi-step autonomous agent pipelines and continuous architecture workflows, tasks execute across distributed runner contexts, invoking heterogeneous LLMs and governance evaluation engines. Without standardized distributed tracing, execution paths remain opaque, hindering diagnostic triage and cost governance.

docs.title: Agentic Profile
docs.text: Applies across all continuous architecture runner workflows, agent tasks, and governance evaluation pipelines where autonomous agents execute discrete reasoning, synthesis, or code-transformation steps.

docs.title: Forces
docs.text: Balances the necessity of granular runtime observability and token cost attribution against span propagation overhead and execution simplicity.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
• Need for granular visibility into multi-agent task execution, LLM call latencies, and token costs
  • Requirement to trace error boundaries across complex sequential and parallel agent pipelines
  • Demand for verifiable operational metrics to enforce continuous architectural governance

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Must adhere to standard OpenTelemetry span propagation specifications
  • Metric collection must not introduce significant runtime latency or block pipeline execution
  • Telemetry schemas must remain provider-agnostic across external LLM and tooling invocations

docs.title: Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Granular tracing introduces slight memory and serialized telemetry transmission overhead
  • Requires agent steps and runner wrappers to consistently propagate trace contexts

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Envelope all agent steps and pipeline orchestrations with OpenTelemetry span instrumentation. Execution runners initialize trace contexts, propagate them across step boundaries, and encapsulate performance and cost data into structured TraceableMetric envelopes, emitting telemetry for downstream analysis and dashboard rendering.

docs.title: Operationalisation
docs.text: Integrate OpenTelemetry instrumentation hooks into execution runners, wrapping agent invocations to automatically capture span context, execution duration, token spend, and error boundaries.

docs.title: Workflow Implications
docs.text:
• Execution runners must initialize and inject OpenTelemetry trace context prior to invoking agent steps
  • Agent steps and model clients must wrap outputs in TraceableMetric envelopes preserving trace identifiers
  • CI/CD pipelines and runtime trace sinks must capture and persist emitted telemetry logs

docs.title: Automation Opportunities
docs.text:
• Automated alerting on agent token cost spikes and step duration regressions
  • Continuous health status scoring derived from aggregated runtime trace metrics in CI
  • Automated identification of flaky or failing agentic steps via distributed span queries

docs.title: Implementation Signals
docs.text: Inclusion of OpenTelemetry SDK dependencies (opentelemetry-api, opentelemetry-sdk) and presence of TraceableMetric schemas in step execution and governance models.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Ratified Reference Architecture in ArchGov and integrated OpenTelemetry dependencies supporting traceable metrics in the runner codebase.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
• Telemetry-observable agent steps implementation using opentelemetry-api and opentelemetry-sdk
  • TraceableMetric data schema encapsulating telemetry in runtime models

docs.title: Supporting Evidence
docs.text: • Ratified Reference Architecture in ArchGov

docs.title: Confidence Basis
docs.text: Empirical implementation in runner codebase backed by ratified reference architecture acceptance in architecture governance review.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Provides end-to-end operational observability into agent workflows at the cost of maintaining span propagation discipline across step implementations.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Comprehensive visibility into agent task execution latency and error boundaries
  • Deterministic accounting of token expenditure and invocation costs across model providers
  • Seamless integration with distributed tracing platforms and governance dashboards

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Trace context loss if custom or third-party agent steps fail to forward OpenTelemetry headers
  • Potential telemetry storage bloat across high-volume automated CI runs if trace sampling is unconfigured

docs.title: Governance Implications
docs.text:
• Mandates OpenTelemetry span compliance as an architectural contract across all agent runner steps
  • Requires runtime metrics to feed continuous architecture health evaluations and audit trails

docs.title: Reuse Notes
docs.text: Globally applicable across continuous architecture runner workflows, agentic task frameworks, and automated governance evaluation pipelines requiring distributed tracing and cost visibility.

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text:
High confidence supported by verified reference architecture ratification and active OpenTelemetry SDK integration.

Level: high

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The pattern is implemented using industry-standard OpenTelemetry APIs and typed metric contracts, ratified in formal architecture governance review.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
What problem does this pattern solve?

It eliminates "string-keyed dictionary" or "dynamic attribute" anti-patterns where pipeline steps depend on invisible or inconsistently defined state. It ensures that inputs, intermediate results, and outputs are discoverable and type-safe across a multi-agent orchestration flow.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
When and where does this pattern appear?

This pattern emerged in the Runner Agentic Intelligence system to manage the high-pressure transition of raw athletic data (FIT/GPX) through multiple processing layers: feature engineering, positioning, intelligence generation, and visualization. It appears in systems where state is progressively enriched by specialized agents or computational engines.

docs.title: Agentic profile
docs.text:
Describe the agentic architecture shape explicitly.

  • System shape: multi-agent
  • Orchestration mode: sequential

docs.title: Agent-to-agent interaction
docs.text:
• Present: true
  • Mechanism: shared-state
  • Evidence: PipelineContext

docs.title: Tool protocols
docs.text:
• MCP: absent
  • Tool calling: present
  • Evidence: Insights Generation (LLM with schema)

docs.title: Optimisation target
docs.text:
• Primary: reliability
  • Secondary: safety, developer-velocity
  • Notes: Ensures that data contracts between agents are explicitly defined in code rather than documentation.

docs.title: Simplicity vs autonomy
docs.text:
• Position: simplicity
  • Rationale: The pattern favors a controlled, predictable state flow over autonomous agent memory, making the system easier to debug and audit.

docs.title: Forces
docs.text:
List the tensions or constraints:

  • Type Safety vs Development Speed: Explicit types require more initial setup but reduce runtime "KeyError" or "AttributeError" failures.
  • Centralization vs Decoupling: A central context creates a structural dependency but provides a single source of truth for the entire execution lifecycle.
  • Memory vs Persistence: The context must distinguish between transient session state and data that must be persisted to the database.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Describe the structural move.

A boundary is introduced between the Orchestrator/Pipeline and the individual Steps. A formal PipelineContext dataclass is defined as the sole carrier of state. Each PipelineStep is defined by a contract that accepts this context, reads only what it needs, and writes results back to specific, pre-defined fields. This separates the logic of "how to compute" from "how to store/pass" data.

docs.title: Implementation signals
docs.text:
Observable signs this pattern exists:

  • A dedicated context.py containing a large dataclass or Pydantic model with fields for every pipeline stage.
  • A base PipelineStep class with an execute(context) method.
  • Steps explicitly casting or extracting data from the context into domain objects before passing them to agents.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Reference specific artefacts:

  • The central typed state holder.
  • The interface enforcing context-based execution.
  • Example of a step extracting data from context and populating results.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Contract Integrity: IDEs and linters can catch missing data dependencies before execution.
  • Observability: The entire state of a run can be captured by serializing a single object.

docs.title: Costs
docs.text:
• Boilerplate: New data points require updates to the central PipelineContext definition.
  • Coupling: Steps are coupled to the context structure even if they only use a fraction of it.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
• Context Bloat: Adding too many transient or unrelated fields makes the object difficult to manage.
  • Parallel Mutation: Without careful design, parallel steps could overwrite the same fields (mitigated here by field-level ownership).

docs.title: Reuse notes
docs.text:
How can this pattern be reused safely?

  • Where it fits: Complex multi-stage pipelines where data is transformed or enriched.
  • Where it does NOT fit: Simple, single-turn agent interactions or systems with very small, stable state requirements.
  • Preconditions: Requires a clear definition of the execution lifecycle and identified boundaries between processing steps.

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: • High → The pattern is consistently applied across the entire core processing logic of the repository, from ingestion to intelligence delivery, and is backed by a dedicated core infrastructure.

docs.title: ADR as Single Source of Truth
Rule
docs.text: Architecture decisions must be recorded and updated only in decision records (ADR); all other representations must be derived from ADR.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Prevents inconsistencies between pattern metadata, AEM, and decision workflows.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• ADR
  • pattern frontmatter
  • AEM generation
  • decision sync workflows

docs.title: Example
docs.text: If a decision is made to adopt a new pattern, the ADR must be updated to reflect this decision. The pattern metadata and AEM must then be updated based on the ADR, ensuring that the ADR remains the single source of truth for architectural decisions.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The Architecture Evolution Map (AEM) must remain consistent with Architecture Decision Records (ADR).

AEM is not limited to decisions, but must never contradict them.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Must follow knowledge/global/rules/rule-decision-status-drives-stage

⸻

Scope Clarification

AEM may include:

  • vision and roadmap items
  • system evolution changes
  • architectural direction

However:

These must not contradict existing decisions.

⸻

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
AEM acts as a control and synthesis layer, combining:

  • decisions (ADR)
  • system evolution
  • intent / vision

Consistency with ADR ensures governance integrity.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text: • architecture_evolution_map

docs.title: Example
docs.text: If an ADR decision is accepted to adopt a new pattern, the AEM must be updated to reflect this change and not contradict it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Benefits:

  • reliable architecture state representation
  • alignment between decisions and roadmap
  • clear governance traceability

Risks if not followed:

  • AEM contradicts ADR
  • misleading architecture state
  • loss of trust in system outputs

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule architecture work authority
docs.text:
Rule

Architecture Work is the authoritative source of architectural planning state; generated artifacts must derive planning status from Architecture Work rather than maintaining independent planning state.

Rationale

Multiple governance inconsistencies were detected when AEM maintained roadmap state that diverged from Architecture Work lifecycle and status metadata.

Applies To

  • Architecture Work Registry
  • AEM generation
  • AID generation
  • Alignment Engine

Example

If Architecture Work status is accepted, the generated AEM must not classify the same work item as proposed.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: Core patterns must represent foundational architectural primitives, not specific strategies or implementations.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Prevents elevation of context-specific or replaceable approaches into the core architecture, maintaining long-term stability.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• pattern-promotion-workflow
  • architect decision review

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Reject promoting dual-path-routing to core because it is one routing strategy, not a universal primitive.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: All decisions must be expressed using a structured YAML decision schema and not as unstructured narrative text.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Enables machine processing, UI rendering, and consistent interpretation across the system.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• applies to ADR only, not rules
  • enforces separation between architect decision and governance approval

docs.title: Output Schema must include:
docs.text:
---
id: "adr-<pattern-id>-<decision-type>-<date>"
knowledgeType: "architecture_decision_record"
pattern_id: "<pattern-id>"
decision_scope: "pattern | system | component | workflow | governance"
decision_target: "<pattern-id | component-name | system-element>"

classification: "core | supporting | project | system | component"

decision:
  type: "<adoption|keep|promotion|demotion|creation|definition|refactor>"
  status: "proposed"  # architect decision status
  decided_by: "architect"
  date: "<YYYY-MM-DD>"

  rationale:
    summary: "<short explanation>"

  evidence:
    strength: "<high|medium|low>"

  confidence: "<high|medium|low>"

governance:
  forum_status: "pending"   # accepted | rejected | deferred"
  forum_decision_date: null # YYYY-MM-DD
---

docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The lifecycle stage of any architecture item must be derived from its decision status. Items with decision.status != "accepted" must not be marked as DONE.

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
• proposed → must map to NEXT or REVIEW
  • accepted → may map to DONE
  • rejected → must not appear as active
  • deferred → must map to FUTURE or DEFER

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• architecture_evolution_map
  • patterns
  • decisions

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Ensures consistency between decision lifecycle and system state representation. Prevents premature promotion of unvalidated architecture elements.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A pattern with decision.status = "proposed" is marked as NEXT, not DONE.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: All architectural decisions must be persisted as structured decision records (ADR) before being reflected in AEM or other artefacts.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Ensures traceability, prevents loss of context, and establishes a single source of truth for architectural decisions.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• promotion-to-decision-records
  • AEM generator

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A pattern promotion creates an ADR file under knowledge/global/decisions before appearing in AEM.

docs.text: • Architecture Governance

Rule
docs.text: Patterns must not be merged or consolidated across different architectural layers.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Preserves architectural clarity by maintaining separation between governance, execution, contracts, and reliability concerns.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• pattern-promotion-workflow
  • pattern refinement

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Do not merge orchestrator-managed-pipeline (execution) with parallel-agent-execution (concurrency strategy).

docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule generated artifacts not authoritative
docs.text:
Rule

Generated governance artifacts must summarize authoritative sources and must not become the authoritative source themselves.

Rationale

Regenerated artifacts lose manually introduced state. Authoritative information must reside in durable source artifacts.

Applies To

  • AEM
  • AID
  • Alignment Reports
  • Generated dashboards

Example

AEM summarizes Architecture Work but does not own backlog state.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: All heuristic-derived patterns must include at least one linked signal as evidence.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Ensures traceability and prevents patterns from being created without grounding in observed behaviour or insights.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• heuristic-to-pattern
  • pattern validation

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A pattern created from signals includes sources.signals with at least one signal id.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
• Intent vs State:
  • Intent artefacts (AID) MUST align with system state (AEM), not reflect it

  • Reflection implies derivation; alignment implies coordination

  • Decision vs System State:

  • Architect decisions (architecture_work.status = accepted) are NOT system state

  • System state exists ONLY when governance.forum_status = accepted

  • Pattern Semantics:

  • Patterns MUST NOT be described as part of the system unless governance-approved

  • Pattern proposals and emerging patterns are NOT system state

  • Lifecycle Terminology:

  • Use "generate" for creation of artefacts
  • Use "persist" for storage of artefacts
  • Use "promote" ONLY when governance-approved transition occurs

  • Avoid ambiguous terms like "becomes" or "turns into" without lifecycle context

  • Consistency:

  • Use consistent terminology across AEM, AID, ADR, and alignment artefacts
  • Avoid semantic drift in repeated runs

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
• Ensures clear distinction between intent, decisions, and system state
  • Prevents semantic drift and misalignment across artefacts
  • Enables accurate traceability and accountability in architecture work
  • Facilitates effective governance and decision-making processes

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• Architecture Intent Documents (AID)
  • Architecture Evolution Maps (AEM)
  • Architecture Decision Records (ADR)
  • Alignment Reports
  • Architecture Work items
  • Governance processes and forums

docs.title: Example
docs.text: • An AID proposes a new pattern based on emerging requirements. The AID describes the pattern proposal and rationale but does NOT claim the pattern is part of the system until it goes through governance and is accepted. The AEM reflects the current state of the system, which does not include the proposed pattern until governance approval is obtained. Alignment reports identify the gap between intent and state but do not treat proposed patterns as system state.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
Global rules follow this hierarchy:

  • global > project > prompt-local

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Rules are hard constraints on architecture work
  • Global rules cannot be violated by project rules
  • Rules should be testable/enforceable
  • Rule conflicts should be detected and resolved

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Pattern maturity and decision lifecycle are distinct but must be interpreted consistently.

  • Pattern maturity reflects knowledge evolution (heuristic → pattern → stable)
  • Decision status reflects governance lifecycle (proposed → accepted → rejected → deferred)

These dimensions must not be conflated.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Must follow knowledge/global/rules/rule-decision-status-drives-stage

Mapping Guidance (Interpretation Only)

Pattern Maturity Decision Status Effective Interpretation exploring none candidate (pre-ADR) exploring proposed validating (NEXT) stable accepted active (DONE) any rejected discarded

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Separating knowledge evolution from governance validation prevents:

  • premature promotion of patterns
  • inconsistent AEM state
  • ambiguity between "observed" vs "approved" architecture

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• patterns
  • architecture_evolution_map
  • architecture_intent_document

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A pattern with maturity "exploring" and decision.status "proposed" is interpreted as a candidate under validation, not an active part of the system. It appears in AEM as NEXT, not DONE, until governance approval is obtained.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Benefits:

  • consistent lifecycle interpretation across CAS
  • reliable AEM stage assignment
  • clearer governance traceability

Risks if not followed:

  • patterns marked DONE without validation
  • drift between ADR and AEM
  • confusion in system state

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Patterns Must Be Created as Supporting
Rule
docs.text: All patterns must be created as supporting by default and never directly as core.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Ensures patterns are validated through evidence and usage before becoming foundational, preventing premature architectural commitments.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• heuristic-to-pattern
  • pattern generation
  • pattern lifecycle

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A pattern derived from signals is created with scope.type = "supporting" and promotion.candidate = true.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This rule defines the precedence hierarchy used to resolve conflicts between rules originating from different sources within the CAS system.

It ensures consistent and predictable behaviour when multiple rules apply to the same context.

docs.title: Precedence Model
docs.text:
The system MUST apply the following precedence order:

Global Rules > Project Rules > Prompt Rules

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Global Rules
    • Define system-wide invariants and governance constraints
    • Act as hard constraints
    • MUST NOT be overridden
  • Project Rules
    • Define context-specific constraints within a project
    • MUST NOT violate global rules
    • May override prompt behaviour where applicable
  • Prompt Rules
    • Define execution-level behaviour
    • Act as default behaviour only
    • MUST defer to both global and project rules

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• In case of conflict, the higher-precedence rule MUST be applied.
  • Lower-precedence rules MUST NOT override higher-precedence rules.
  • Conflicts MUST be:
    • detected (via rules-conflict-detector)
    • resolved using this precedence model
    • explicitly surfaced in governance artefacts

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
A clear precedence hierarchy prevents:

  • inconsistent system behaviour
  • duplication of governance logic
  • ambiguity in rule interpretation

It enables scalable governance across multiple projects and prompts.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• rule conflict detection and resolution
  • prompt execution behaviour
  • AEM and AID generation
  • any system component interpreting rules

docs.title: Example
docs.text: If a global rule mandates that all patterns must be classified according to the Pattern Classification Framework, a project rule cannot override this requirement. However, a project rule could specify that for a particular project, certain pattern categories are preferred, as long as it does not violate the global classification requirement. Prompt rules could then specify how to apply these classifications during execution, but must defer to both the global and project rules.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Benefits

  • deterministic rule resolution
  • consistent behaviour across all components
  • reduced duplication in prompts
  • improved traceability and explainability

Risks if not followed

  • conflicting outputs across prompts
  • silent overrides of critical constraints
  • governance drift and loss of trust in system outputs

⸻

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: Pattern promotion to core must be supported by strong evidence, preferably from multiple sources or systems.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Prevents weak or context-specific patterns from becoming foundational, ensuring the core architecture remains stable and reliable.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• pattern-promotion-workflow
  • decision-making

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A pattern observed in only one project is marked as "needs more evidence" rather than promoted.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule shared knowledge workspace
docs.text:
Rule

Projects participate in a shared Knowledge Workspace and must not create duplicate workspace-level governance structures when an existing workspace is available.

Rationale

Shared governance intelligence depends on reusable workspace assets and idempotent onboarding.

Applies To

  • Bootstrap
  • Knowledge Provider
  • Workspace initialization

Example

Project onboarding may create projects// but must not recreate global/, runtime/, or templates/ if they already exist.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: A candidate signal must only be promoted to a pattern when it satisfies all mandatory criteria and is supported by observable evidence across the system.

docs.title: Promotion Criteria
docs.text:
A signal is eligible for promotion only if ALL of the following are satisfied:

  • Recurrence (mandatory) The signal appears multiple times across:
  • architecture_work entries, OR
  • alignment findings, OR

  • repeated conversational emergence

  • System Impact (mandatory) The signal affects at least one of:

  • system behaviour
  • governance
  • execution flow
  • contracts

  • consistency / drift

  • Reusability (mandatory) The insight applies beyond a single instance or local context

  • Stability (mandatory) The signal is not transient, tool-specific, or one-off

docs.title: Evidence Requirement
docs.text:
At least one of the following must support the signal:

  • Referenced in alignment findings (e.g. related_signals)
  • Captured in architecture_work
  • Repeated across multiple runs or interactions

docs.title: Non-Promotion Rule
docs.text:
If the above criteria are not fully satisfied:

  • The signal MUST remain a candidate signal
  • It MUST NOT be promoted to a pattern
  • It MAY be refined or re-evaluated in future iterations

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: To prevent premature or noisy pattern creation, promotion must be based on consistent, system-level signals rather than isolated observations, ensuring patterns represent stable and reusable architectural knowledge.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• signal → pattern promotion workflow
  • architecture_work decision-making
  • alignment-engine (candidate signal evaluation)
  • architecture-work-to-adr validation

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A signal like "generators behave inconsistently without explicit contracts" is promoted because it:

  • appears across multiple runs (recurrence)
  • impacts execution and governance (impact)
  • applies to all generators (reusability)
  • remains valid across tools (stability)
  • is supported by alignment findings and architecture work (evidence)

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: All architectural decisions must be proposed by the system and explicitly accepted, rejected, or deferred by an architect.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Maintains human-in-the-loop control to preserve architectural integrity and avoid incorrect automated decisions.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• pattern-promotion-workflow
  • decision records (ADR)
  • AEM generation

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A promotion output sets decision.status = "proposed" and requires manual update to "accepted".

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Architecture Governance

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
All runtime-native workflows must comply with the CAS Workflow Execution Model.

Specifically:

  • CAS Runner is responsible for orchestration.
  • Workflows are responsible for reasoning.
  • Knowledge Providers are responsible for knowledge access.
  • Prompt contracts remain the authoritative source of workflow reasoning behaviour.
  • Workflows must consume context supplied by CAS Runner.
  • Workflows must not perform repository discovery or direct knowledge workspace scanning.
  • Workflows must not assume repository structure.
  • Workflows must not implement orchestration responsibilities that belong to CAS Runner.
  • Workflow outputs must conform to their declared schema contracts.
  • Runtime onboarding must follow the lifecycle and responsibility boundaries defined by the CAS Workflow Execution Model.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
CAS is evolving from a collection of manually executed prompts into a governance platform with runtime-native capabilities.

Without a common execution model, workflows risk embedding responsibilities that belong to orchestration, knowledge access, or runtime management. This creates inconsistent onboarding approaches, duplicated logic, tighter coupling to repository structures, and reduced portability across execution environments.

The Workflow Execution Model establishes a consistent separation of concerns:

text Knowledge Provider ↓ Provides Knowledge CAS Runner ↓ Orchestrates Workflow ↓ Reasons Schema ↓ Validates Outputs

This separation improves maintainability, onboarding consistency, automation readiness, and governance scalability.

docs.title: Applies To
docs.text:
• Runtime-native workflows
  • Workflow onboarding efforts
  • CAS Runner capabilities
  • Discovery workflows
  • Governance workflows
  • Intelligence workflows
  • Publication workflows
  • Future workflow registrations
  • Runtime orchestration implementations

Examples include:

  • conversation-to-architecture-work
  • vision-to-architecture-work
  • discovery-to-architecture-work
  • signal-to-pattern-proposal
  • cross-aid-synthesis

docs.title: Compliant
docs.text:
text CAS Runner ↓ Loads Conversation Context Workflow ↓ Generates Architecture Work CAS Runner ↓ Persists Output

The workflow receives context and performs reasoning only.

docs.title: Non-Compliant
docs.text:
text Workflow ↓ Scans knowledge/projects/** ↓ Discovers Inputs ↓ Generates Output ↓ Writes Files Directly

The workflow performs repository discovery and persistence responsibilities that belong to CAS Runner, violating the Workflow Execution Model.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
Violations should be identified during:

  • Workflow onboarding reviews
  • Architecture reviews
  • Governance assessments
  • Alignment evaluations
  • Runtime capability validation

New runtime workflows should demonstrate compliance before being promoted to first-class CAS capabilities.

docs.title: Evidence & Conclusions
docs.text:
• The project ea4all-agentic-build possesses strong foundational instructions and operational guides (README.md, GEMINI.md, CLAUDE.md) defining specification-driven development, sub-agent structures (ea4all_apm, ea4all_gra, ea4all_sya, ea4all_vqa, pmo_crew, ea4all_mcp, ea4all_indexer), and tech stack constraints (Python 3.12, Gradio, LangChain, LangGraph).
  • No project-specific Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), Architecture Intent Documents (AIDs), or Architecture Evolution Maps (AEMs) currently exist in the target repository.
  • Global CAS governance policies and decision precedents (e.g. ADR-067 Target Evidence Isolation) are active, but local governance records for ea4all-agentic-build have not yet been formalized.
  • System architecture is well-articulated in user documentation, but project-level decision persistence and formal architectural tracking require bootstrapping.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: The ea4all-agentic-build system is an agentic Architecture Intelligence Platform utilizing LangGraph, CrewAI, and specialized sub-agents to automate EA analysis and governance. Operational guides (README.md, GEMINI.md, CLAUDE.md) are well-articulated, but formal local governance persistence (AID, AEM, project ADRs) is emerging/low, leaving active orchestration code without formal project decision anchors.

docs.title: Architecture Evolution Summary
docs.text: The project is transitioning from operational documentation and initial code implementation toward formalized specification-driven governance. Initial Architecture Intent Document (AID) and Architecture Work items have been proposed to anchor agent boundaries and persist decision records.

docs.title: Architecture Evolution
docs.text: Evolutionary trajectory is moving from code-first agent graph implementation toward structured, specification-driven architecture isolation in accordance with ADR-067 evidence isolation principles.

docs.title: Capability Landscape
docs.text: Core active capabilities include multi-agent orchestration (LangGraph, CrewAI) and sub-agent modules (ea4all_apm, ea4all_gra, ea4all_sya, ea4all_vqa, pmo_crew, ea4all_mcp). Capabilities are operationally defined but lack project-level AID/ADR formalization.

docs.title: Capability Dependencies
docs.text: Sub-agent runtime relies on Python 3.12, Gradio, LangChain, and LangGraph. Governance capabilities depend on bootstrapping project-level AID and AEM governance artifacts.

docs.title: Initiative Landscape
docs.text: Active initiatives include 'Baseline Discovery' (Bootstrapping AID and initial AEM) and 'Governance Foundation' (Formalizing LangGraph orchestration ADR and resolving pending pattern ADRs).

docs.title: Alignment Summary

docs.title: Alignment Findings
docs.text:
• [HIGH] The project currently relies entirely on inherited global CAS ADRs, with zero project-specific architectural decision records. This contradicts the strategic intent for project-isolated governance and local decision persistence.
  • Recommendation: Establish and populate a project-specific ADR framework to capture local workflow orchestration and evidence intake decisions.
  • [HIGH] The system lacks an authoritative inventory of currently implemented Python modules and entrypoints. While ADR-038 has been accepted, the inventory.yaml has not yet been initialized, leaving the runtime state undocumented.
  • Recommendation: Initialize inventory.yaml deterministically via git diff and establish incremental update mechanisms as defined in ADR-038.
  • [HIGH] The core workflow remains a single monolithic component ('ea4all-automation-main-comp'), failing to decompose into discrete intake, classification, and structured synthesis modules as mandated by the vision architecture blueprint.
  • Recommendation: Decompose the monolithic core workflow into distinct modules aligned with the Spec-Kit governance skills and vision blueprint.
  • [MEDIUM] While ADR-067 (Target Project Evidence Isolation) and ADR-075 (Architecture State Forensic Diagnostic) are accepted, their implementation into the project's operational governance pipeline is still in the READY state, leaving evidence intake workflows unenforced.
  • Recommendation: Accelerate implementation of evidence isolation and forensic diagnostic gates to align operational governance with accepted ADRs.

docs.title: Speckit Assess Define Workflow
docs.text:
1. State the problem in one or two sentences: who is affected, what hurts today, under what conditions, and why it matters now. Keep it in the problem space — no features, no architecture.
  2. Identify users and stakeholders. Users experience the problem; stakeholders decide, fund, or are impacted. Cite research where available; mark invented entries [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: …].
  3. Set goals — the outcomes that would make solving this worthwhile.
  4. Set non-goals — what is explicitly out of scope, to bound the work and prevent creep.
  5. Define success metrics — how you would know it worked. Prefer measurable signals; use qualitative ones only when necessary, and label them as such.
  6. Establish a baseline — what happens if nothing is built (the cost of inaction). This is what /speckit-assess-decide weighs against.
  7. Carry forward open questions from intake/research that must be resolved before or during specification.

docs.title: Speckit Assess Shape Workflow
docs.text:
1. Generate 2–3 distinct options, spanning the trade-off space. Always include a lightweight "smallest thing that could work" option and, where relevant, a "do nothing / buy instead of build" option. Each option:
  2. Recommend one option with a short rationale tied to the problem's goals and metrics — or explicitly recommend not proceeding if no option clears the bar.
  3. Bound the concept: restate what is explicitly out of scope for the recommended option (inherited from non-goals plus anything newly excluded).
  4. List the assumptions the recommendation depends on, so they can be validated during specification.

docs.title: Speckit Assess Research Workflow
docs.text:
1. Explicit slug (slug=…, --slug …, or an obvious token) — normalize it (see Slug safety below).
  2. Conversation context — if this session just ran /speckit-assess-intake, reuse the slug it reported. Confirm by checking that .specify/assessments/<slug>/intake.md exists; if not, fall through.
  3. Interactive — ask the user for the slug and wait.
  4. Automated — if exactly one assessment directory exists, use it; otherwise stop and ask.
  5. Users & demand — Who actually has this problem, and how strong is the signal? Support tickets, interviews, usage data, requests. Distinguish stated wants from observed behavior.
  6. Prior art — Has this been tried before, here or elsewhere? Existing internal features, past specs/decisions in .specify/, competitor products, open-source alternatives. Why did prior attempts succeed or fail?
  7. Market & context — Trends, alternatives users cope with today, the cost of doing nothing.
  8. Data & constraints — Relevant metrics, volumes, compliance/legal factors, platform limits.
  9. Evidence quality — For each finding, tag confidence high | medium | low and whether it is cited (source given) or assumption (no source).

docs.title: Speckit Taskstoissues Workflow
docs.text:
1. Run .specify/scripts/bash/check-prerequisites.sh --json --require-tasks --include-tasks from repo root and parse FEATURE_DIR and AVAILABLE_DOCS list. All paths must be absolute. For single quotes in args like "I'm Groot", use escape syntax: e.g 'I'\''m Groot' (or double-quote if possible: "I'm Groot").
  2. IF EXISTS: Load .specify/memory/constitution.md for project principles and governance constraints.
  3. From the executed script, extract the path to tasks.
  4. Get the Git remote by running:
  5. Fetch existing issues for deduplication: Before creating anything, build the set of task IDs you are about to process from tasks.md (each is a T followed by at least three digits, e.g. T001 — /speckit-converge assigns new IDs with T{M+1:03d}, which is a floor rather than a cap, so once a file has more than 999 tasks the IDs are four digits or longer). Then use the GitHub MCP server's list_issues tool to look for issues that already cover those IDs. Do not pass a state value, since omitting it makes the tool return both open and closed issues. Request perPage: 100 to keep the number of calls down, and since the tool uses cursor-based pagination, request pages with the after parameter (using the endCursor from the previous response). For each issue title, match it against the task ID pattern \bT\d{3,}\b (the {3,} accepts four-digit and longer IDs — with \d{3} a title containing T1000 would not match at all, because the trailing \b cannot fall between two digits, so that task would be silently neither deduplicated nor created; word boundaries still stop a token like ST001 from matching, and force the whole digit run to be consumed so T100 can never match inside T1000; this also recognises titles written as T001 ..., T001: ... or [T001] ...) and, when it matches one of your task IDs, mark that ID as already having an issue. Stop paginating as soon as every task ID has been matched, or when there are no more pages, so you do not keep fetching the whole repository's issue history once all task IDs are accounted for. This bounds the number of calls on repos with large issue histories and still prevents duplicates when the command is re-run after tasks.md is regenerated or the skill is re-invoked.
  6. For each task in the list, use the GitHub MCP server to create a new issue in the repository that is representative of the Git remote. Task lines in tasks.md start with a markdown checkbox, so first strip the leading - [ ] (and any [P] / [US#] markers) to recover the task ID and its description. Create the issue with a single canonical title of the form T001: <description>, with the ID written once followed by the task description (for example, the line - [ ] T001 Create project structure becomes the title T001: Create project structure).

  27. Number questions sequentially (Q1, Q2, Q3 - max 3 total)
  28. Present all questions together before waiting for responses
  29. Wait for user to respond with their choices for all questions (e.g., "Q1: A, Q2: Custom - [details], Q3: B")
  30. Update the spec by replacing each [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] marker with the user's selected or provided answer
  31. Re-run validation after all clarifications are resolved
  32. Make informed guesses: Use context, industry standards, and common patterns to fill gaps
  33. Document assumptions: Record reasonable defaults in the Assumptions section
  34. Limit clarifications: Maximum 3 [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] markers - use only for critical decisions that:
  35. Prioritize clarifications: scope > security/privacy > user experience > technical details
  36. Think like a tester: Every vague requirement should fail the "testable and unambiguous" checklist item
  37. Common areas needing clarification (only if no reasonable default exists):
  38. Measurable: Include specific metrics (time, percentage, count, rate)
  39. Technology-agnostic: No mention of frameworks, languages, databases, or tools
  40. User-focused: Describe outcomes from user/business perspective, not system internals
  41. Verifiable: Can be tested/validated without knowing implementation details

docs.title: Speckit Assess Intake Workflow
docs.text:
1. Pasted text — a one-liner, a paragraph, a stakeholder ask, meeting notes, a ticket body.
  2. A URL — a link to an issue, doc, thread, or page describing the idea. Apply the URL Trust Policy below before fetching.
  3. A codebase pointer — phrasing like "an idea for this repo" or a path. Read enough of the repository to record what the idea relates to.
  4. A mix of the above.
  5. User-provided slug: If the user explicitly passes a slug (e.g., slug=offline-mode, --slug offline-mode, or an obvious slug-like token), normalize it: lowercase; convert runs of whitespace/underscores to -; keep only lowercase letters a–z, digits 0–9, and -; drop every other character (including ., /, \); collapse repeated -; strip leading/trailing -. Do not append timestamps or numbers.
  6. Interactive mode (a human is driving): If no slug was provided, ask the user and wait. Suggest a 2–4 word kebab-case candidate derived from the idea as a default.
  7. Automated / non-interactive mode (no human to ask): Generate a concise slug yourself (2–4 kebab-case words). The generated slug MUST produce a unique directory — if .specify/assessments/<slug>/ already exists, append the shortest disambiguating suffix (-2, -3, …) or a short ISO-style date (-20260715). Never overwrite an existing assessment directory.
  8. Refuse outright (do not fetch, do not prompt). Record the URL and reason in intake.md:
  9. Fetch without prompting when the host is a widely-used public source: github.com, gist.github.com, gitlab.com, bitbucket.org, *.atlassian.net, linear.app, notion.so, *.notion.site, docs.google.com, stackoverflow.com, *.stackexchange.com.
  10. Otherwise the host is unrecognized:
  11. Capture the idea, redacting secrets. Preserve the original wording (quoted) plus the source (URL, pasted block, or repo path) — but apply the same sanitization as the Source field inside the quoted text too: sanitize any credential-bearing URL and redact tokens, passwords, API keys, or cookies. Never persist a secret just because it appeared in the original.
  12. Restate it in one or two neutral sentences. What is being proposed, in plain language, without endorsing or dismissing it.
  13. Record origin and context. Who raised it, when, and any triggering event (a complaint, an outage, a sales ask, a strategy shift). Mark unknowns as [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: …].
  14. Note the idea type so downstream stages know what to weigh: new-capability | improvement | fix | exploration | cost-saving | compliance | other.
  15. List first-glance unknowns — the obvious questions that must be answered before anyone decides. Do not answer them here.
  16. Write the intake note to ASSESS_DIR/intake.md:
  17. Report back with:

docs.title: Flow: Speckit Assess Define Workflow (flow:governance:speckit-assess-define:execution-workflow)
docs.text:
• Type: governance
  • Sequence:
  • State the problem in one or two sentences: who is affected, what hurts today, under what conditions, and why it matters now. Keep it in the problem space — no features, no architecture.
  • Identify users and stakeholders. Users experience the problem; stakeholders decide, fund, or are impacted. Cite research where available; mark invented entries [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: …].
  • Set goals — the outcomes that would make solving this worthwhile.
  • Set non-goals — what is explicitly out of scope, to bound the work and prevent creep.
  • Define success metrics — how you would know it worked. Prefer measurable signals; use qualitative ones only when necessary, and label them as such.
  • Establish a baseline — what happens if nothing is built (the cost of inaction). This is what /speckit-assess-decide weighs against.
  • Carry forward open questions from intake/research that must be resolved before or during specification.

docs.title: Flow: Speckit Assess Shape Workflow (flow:governance:speckit-assess-shape:execution-workflow)
docs.text:
• Type: governance
  • Sequence:
  • Generate 2–3 distinct options, spanning the trade-off space. Always include a lightweight "smallest thing that could work" option and, where relevant, a "do nothing / buy instead of build" option. Each option:
  • Recommend one option with a short rationale tied to the problem's goals and metrics — or explicitly recommend not proceeding if no option clears the bar.
  • Bound the concept: restate what is explicitly out of scope for the recommended option (inherited from non-goals plus anything newly excluded).
  • List the assumptions the recommendation depends on, so they can be validated during specification.

docs.text:

docs.title: Flow: Speckit Assess Research Workflow (flow:governance:speckit-assess-research:execution-workflow)
docs.text:
• Type: governance
  • Sequence:
  • Explicit slug (slug=…, --slug …, or an obvious token) — normalize it (see Slug safety below).
  • Conversation context — if this session just ran /speckit-assess-intake, reuse the slug it reported. Confirm by checking that .specify/assessments/<slug>/intake.md exists; if not, fall through.
  • Interactive — ask the user for the slug and wait.
  • Automated — if exactly one assessment directory exists, use it; otherwise stop and ask.
  • Users & demand — Who actually has this problem, and how strong is the signal? Support tickets, interviews, usage data, requests. Distinguish stated wants from observed behavior.
  • Prior art — Has this been tried before, here or elsewhere? Existing internal features, past specs/decisions in .specify/, competitor products, open-source alternatives. Why did prior attempts succeed or fail?
  • Market & context — Trends, alternatives users cope with today, the cost of doing nothing.
  • Data & constraints — Relevant metrics, volumes, compliance/legal factors, platform limits.
  • Evidence quality — For each finding, tag confidence high | medium | low and whether it is cited (source given) or assumption (no source).

docs.title: Flow: Speckit Taskstoissues Workflow (flow:governance:speckit-taskstoissues:execution-workflow)
docs.text:
• Type: governance
  • Sequence:
  • Run .specify/scripts/bash/check-prerequisites.sh --json --require-tasks --include-tasks from repo root and parse FEATURE_DIR and AVAILABLE_DOCS list. All paths must be absolute. For single quotes in args like "I'm Groot", use escape syntax: e.g 'I'\''m Groot' (or double-quote if possible: "I'm Groot").
  • IF EXISTS: Load .specify/memory/constitution.md for project principles and governance constraints.
  • From the executed script, extract the path to tasks.
  • Get the Git remote by running:
  • Fetch existing issues for deduplication: Before creating anything, build the set of task IDs you are about to process from tasks.md (each is a T followed by at least three digits, e.g. T001 — /speckit-converge assigns new IDs with T{M+1:03d}, which is a floor rather than a cap, so once a file has more than 999 tasks the IDs are four digits or longer). Then use the GitHub MCP server's list_issues tool to look for issues that already cover those IDs. Do not pass a state value, since omitting it makes the tool return both open and closed issues. Request perPage: 100 to keep the number of calls down, and since the tool uses cursor-based pagination, request pages with the after parameter (using the endCursor from the previous response). For each issue title, match it against the task ID pattern \bT\d{3,}\b (the {3,} accepts four-digit and longer IDs — with \d{3} a title containing T1000 would not match at all, because the trailing \b cannot fall between two digits, so that task would be silently neither deduplicated nor created; word boundaries still stop a token like ST001 from matching, and force the whole digit run to be consumed so T100 can never match inside T1000; this also recognises titles written as T001 ..., T001: ... or [T001] ...) and, when it matches one of your task IDs, mark that ID as already having an issue. Stop paginating as soon as every task ID has been matched, or when there are no more pages, so you do not keep fetching the whole repository's issue history once all task IDs are accounted for. This bounds the number of calls on repos with large issue histories and still prevents duplicates when the command is re-run after tasks.md is regenerated or the skill is re-invoked.
  • For each task in the list, use the GitHub MCP server to create a new issue in the repository that is representative of the Git remote. Task lines in tasks.md start with a markdown checkbox, so first strip the leading - [ ] (and any [P] / [US#] markers) to recover the task ID and its description. Create the issue with a single canonical title of the form T001: <description>, with the ID written once followed by the task description (for example, the line - [ ] T001 Create project structure becomes the title T001: Create project structure).

docs.text:
• Type: governance

  • Run .specify/scripts/bash/check-prerequisites.sh --json --paths-only from repo root once (combined --json --paths-only mode / -Json -PathsOnly). Parse minimal JSON payload fields:
  • IF EXISTS: Load .specify/memory/constitution.md for project principles and governance constraints.
  • Load the current spec file. Perform a structured ambiguity & coverage scan using this taxonomy. For each category, mark status: Clear / Partial / Missing. Produce an internal coverage map used for prioritization (do not output raw map unless no questions will be asked).
  • Generate (internally) a prioritized queue of candidate clarification questions (maximum 5). Do NOT output them all at once. Apply these constraints:
  • Sequential questioning loop (interactive):
  • Integration after EACH accepted answer (incremental update approach):
  • Validation (performed after EACH write plus final pass):
  • Write the updated spec back to FEATURE_SPEC.
  • Re-validate Spec Quality Checklist (if it exists):
  • Read the checklist file.
  • Identify all GitHub task-list checkbox lines — lines matching - [ ], - [x], or - [X] (case-insensitive, tolerant of leading whitespace for nested items) outside of code fences. Ignore all other content (headings, notes, non-checkbox bullets, metadata).
  • For each checkbox line, record its current marker state (checked or unchecked) and item text into a before-snapshot list.
  • Re-evaluate each checkbox item against the updated spec (the version just saved in step 7).
  • For each checkbox item, update only if the checked/unchecked state actually changes:
  • Save the updated checklist file. Only toggle the [ ]/[x] marker portion of checkbox lines whose state changed. All other file content — headings, metadata, notes, line ordering, whitespace — must remain unchanged to avoid noisy diffs.
  • Compare the before-snapshot with the current state to compute three lists for the Completion Report:
  • Record the before/after pass counts as checked/total checkbox items (e.g., "12/16 → 15/16 items passing").

docs.title: Flow: Speckit Specify Workflow (flow:governance:speckit-specify:execution-workflow)
docs.text:
• Type: governance
  • Sequence:
  • Generate a concise short name (2-4 words) for the feature:
  • Branch creation (optional, via hook):
  • Create the spec feature directory:
  • If the user explicitly provided SPECIFY_FEATURE_DIRECTORY (e.g., via environment variable, argument, or configuration), use it as-is
  • Otherwise, auto-generate it under specs/:
  • Load the resolved active spec-template file to understand required sections.
  • IF EXISTS: Load .specify/memory/constitution.md for project principles and governance constraints.
  • Follow this execution flow:
  • Parse user description from arguments
  • Extract key concepts from description
  • For unclear aspects:
  • Fill User Scenarios & Testing section
  • Generate Functional Requirements
  • Define Success Criteria
  • Identify Key Entities (if data involved)
  • Return: SUCCESS (spec ready for planning)
  • Write the specification to SPEC_FILE using the template structure, replacing placeholders with concrete details derived from the feature description (arguments) while preserving section order and headings.
  • Specification Quality Validation: After writing the initial spec, validate it against quality criteria:
  • List the failing items and specific issues
  • Update the spec to address each issue
  • Re-run validation until all items pass (max 3 iterations)
  • If still failing after 3 iterations, document remaining issues in checklist notes and warn user
  • Extract all [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: ...] markers from the spec
  • LIMIT CHECK: If more than 3 markers exist, keep only the 3 most critical (by scope/security/UX impact) and make informed guesses for the rest
  • For each clarification needed (max 3), present options to user in this format:
  • CRITICAL - Table Formatting: Ensure markdown tables are properly formatted:
  • Number questions sequentially (Q1, Q2, Q3 - max 3 total)
  • Present all questions together before waiting for responses
  • Wait for user to respond with their choices for all questions (e.g., "Q1: A, Q2: Custom - [details], Q3: B")
  • Update the spec by replacing each [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] marker with the user's selected or provided answer
  • Re-run validation after all clarifications are resolved
  • Make informed guesses: Use context, industry standards, and common patterns to fill gaps
  • Document assumptions: Record reasonable defaults in the Assumptions section
  • Limit clarifications: Maximum 3 [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] markers - use only for critical decisions that:
  • Prioritize clarifications: scope > security/privacy > user experience > technical details
  • Think like a tester: Every vague requirement should fail the "testable and unambiguous" checklist item
  • Common areas needing clarification (only if no reasonable default exists):
  • Measurable: Include specific metrics (time, percentage, count, rate)
  • Technology-agnostic: No mention of frameworks, languages, databases, or tools
  • User-focused: Describe outcomes from user/business perspective, not system internals
  • Verifiable: Can be tested/validated without knowing implementation details

docs.title: Flow: Speckit Assess Intake Workflow (flow:governance:speckit-assess-intake:execution-workflow)
docs.text:
• Type: governance
  • Sequence:
  • Pasted text — a one-liner, a paragraph, a stakeholder ask, meeting notes, a ticket body.
  • A URL — a link to an issue, doc, thread, or page describing the idea. Apply the URL Trust Policy below before fetching.
  • A codebase pointer — phrasing like "an idea for this repo" or a path. Read enough of the repository to record what the idea relates to.
  • A mix of the above.
  • User-provided slug: If the user explicitly passes a slug (e.g., slug=offline-mode, --slug offline-mode, or an obvious slug-like token), normalize it: lowercase; convert runs of whitespace/underscores to -; keep only lowercase letters a–z, digits 0–9, and -; drop every other character (including ., /, \); collapse repeated -; strip leading/trailing -. Do not append timestamps or numbers.
  • Interactive mode (a human is driving): If no slug was provided, ask the user and wait. Suggest a 2–4 word kebab-case candidate derived from the idea as a default.
  • Automated / non-interactive mode (no human to ask): Generate a concise slug yourself (2–4 kebab-case words). The generated slug MUST produce a unique directory — if .specify/assessments/<slug>/ already exists, append the shortest disambiguating suffix (-2, -3, …) or a short ISO-style date (-20260715). Never overwrite an existing assessment directory.
  • Refuse outright (do not fetch, do not prompt). Record the URL and reason in intake.md:
  • Fetch without prompting when the host is a widely-used public source: github.com, gist.github.com, gitlab.com, bitbucket.org, *.atlassian.net, linear.app, notion.so, *.notion.site, docs.google.com, stackoverflow.com, *.stackexchange.com.
  • Otherwise the host is unrecognized:
  • Capture the idea, redacting secrets. Preserve the original wording (quoted) plus the source (URL, pasted block, or repo path) — but apply the same sanitization as the Source field inside the quoted text too: sanitize any credential-bearing URL and redact tokens, passwords, API keys, or cookies. Never persist a secret just because it appeared in the original.
  • Restate it in one or two neutral sentences. What is being proposed, in plain language, without endorsing or dismissing it.
  • Record origin and context. Who raised it, when, and any triggering event (a complaint, an outage, a sales ask, a strategy shift). Mark unknowns as [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: …].
  • Note the idea type so downstream stages know what to weigh: new-capability | improvement | fix | exploration | cost-saving | compliance | other.
  • List first-glance unknowns — the obvious questions that must be answered before anyone decides. Do not answer them here.
  • Write the intake note to ASSESS_DIR/intake.md:
  • Report back with:

docs.title: Check for exemptions in commit messages
docs.text: EXEMPT=$(git log --format=%B -n 1 ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} | grep -E "[skip-governance]|[bugfix]" || true) if [ -n "$EXEMPT" ]; then echo "[CAS][SKIP] Exemption found in commit message: $EXEMPT" exit 0 fi

docs.title: Get list of changed files
docs.text:
CHANGED_FILES=$(git diff --name-only origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }})

HAS_SRC_CHANGES=false HAS_SPEC_CHANGES=false

for file in $CHANGED_FILES; do if [[ $file == src/ ]]; then HAS_SRC_CHANGES=true fi if [[ $file == specs/ ]] || [[ $file == .specify/* ]]; then HAS_SPEC_CHANGES=true fi done

if [ "$HAS_SRC_CHANGES" = true ] && [ "$HAS_SPEC_CHANGES" = false ]; then echo "[CAS][ERROR] Code changes detected in 'src/' without corresponding specification in 'specs/' or '.specify/'." echo "[CAS][HINT] Please create a specification before implementing features. Use '[bugfix]' in the commit message to bypass for trivial fixes." exit 1 fi

echo "[CAS][SUCCESS] SDD validation passed." ` - Depends On: step:1:checkout-code

docs.text:
• Repository architecture reconstructed via forensic diagnostic demonstrates high empirical evidence coverage (100%) for core discovered components.
  • Primary codebase is a Python container ('ea4all-automation-core') exposing an entry point component 'ea4all-automation-main-comp' rooted at 'src/'.

  • Operational context files (CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md) enforce strict CAS governance rules: SDD spec creation, surgical edits, and automated test execution with pytest.
  • The project vision establishes clear operating principles: human architectural accountability, deterministic execution where practical, and evidence before narrative.
  • Current governance evidence consists exclusively of inherited global CAS platform ADRs; zero project-specific ADRs or Architecture Work items are recorded for ea4all-automation.

docs.title: Governance Maturity
docs.text: Foundational assets are robust, featuring an explicit vision document, agent operating instructions, and an empirically reconstructed 4-pillar architecture state. However, governance evidence maturity is nascent: there are no project-scoped ADRs, decision logs, or capability inventories established specifically for ea4all-automation, relying instead on inherited global CAS decisions.

docs.title: Identified Gaps & Opportunities
docs.text:
• Absence of project-scoped Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) documenting core component contracts, interfaces, and framework choices.
  • Discovered components and flows are limited to generic placeholders ('ea4all-automation-main-comp') and SDD validation; specific operational pipeline implementations need explicit decomposition.
  • Lack of a local Runtime Capability Inventory (inventory.yaml) to track capability extraction deltas as prescribed by ADR-038.
  • Opportunity to establish initial project-specific baseline promotion and formalize evidence intake workflows aligned with the EA Automation Vision.

docs.title: Strategic Vision
docs.text:
• What we are building: A composable, lightweight operating architecture for Enterprise Architecture automation that transforms proven EA operating model elements into reusable, governed workflows.
  • Why it exists: To make EA practice more evidence-led, repeatable, and scalable while preserving human judgment, accountability, and stakeholder engagement for consequential decisions.

docs.title: Project Context
docs.text: primary_context: ea4all-automation aw_count: 6 alignment_findings: 3

docs.title: Current State Alignment
docs.text: The system is partially aligned with strategic intent. Core empirical evidence coverage is high, but governance maturity is nascent. The architecture currently exhibits a structural monolith in the core workflow and relies entirely on inherited global CAS ADRs, creating a gap between accepted strategic decisions and operational reality.

docs.title: Focus Areas / Roadmap
docs.text:
• Initialize Project Runtime Capability Inventory to establish deterministic baseline and track implementation deltas.
  • Establish Project-Specific Architecture Decision Record Framework to capture local workflow orchestration and evidence intake decisions.
  • Refine Component Boundary Decomposition for Core Workflow by splitting the monolithic component into discrete intake, classification, and structured synthesis modules.
  • Operationalize Evidence Isolation and Forensic Diagnostic gates to align CI-level validation with accepted ADRs.
  • Validate conceptual architecture blueprint through real delivery, iterating on methods and generalizing successful automation candidates into reusable SOPs and Skills.

docs.title: Gaps & Tensions (Risks)
docs.text:
• Absence of project-scoped ADRs obscures local trade-offs and violates single-source-of-truth standards.
  • Lack of authoritative runtime capability inventory prevents automated delta verification and deterministic extraction.
  • Structural monolith in the core workflow contradicts the composable pipeline vision and separation of concerns.
  • Governance framework adoption (ADR-067, ADR-075) is accepted but operationally pending, creating a temporary enforcement gap.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Start with a real delivery problem, not a technology opportunity.
  • Formulate a clear hypothesis before automating.
  • Build the smallest useful solution and validate it in real delivery.
  • Evidence before narrative; make uncertainty explicit.
  • Use AI as augmentation, not as unaccountable authority.
  • Keep human review mandatory for consequential judgement.
  • Prefer guardrails and actionable feedback over gatekeeping.
  • Learn, iterate, generalise, replace, or stop each automation based on demonstrated value.

docs.title: Emergent Heuristics
docs.text: decision_tracing: Material decisions must be traceable from context and evidence to consequences. automation_threshold: A repeatable delivery problem must show sufficient frequency, effort, risk, or value before it is generalised into a platform capability. governance_evolution: Shift from global CAS dependency to project-specific governance as local evidence and decisions accumulate. workflow_adaptation: Workflow depth and automation scope must be tailored to decision risk, complexity, and available evidence, not forced into rigid templates.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: The ea4all-automation project is currently in a foundational baseline discovery phase. Empirical discovery demonstrates 100% evidence coverage for existing repository assets, supported by active Specification-Driven Development (SDD) CI validation controls. However, governance maturity is nascent: the project currently operates without local Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) or an authoritative capability inventory (inventory.yaml), relying entirely on inherited global CAS standards. Structurally, the codebase remains a monolithic Python entrypoint awaiting decomposition into the intake, classification, and synthesis stages defined in the target architecture intent.

docs.title: Architecture Evolution Summary
docs.text: The project has evolved from an uncharacterized codebase into a forensically baselined system with explicit architectural intent and formal alignment reporting. Initial architecture work candidates have been derived to transition the project from passive reliance on global platform governance to active local governance scaffolding and modular decomposition.

docs.title: Architecture Evolution
docs.text: The architecture is transitioning from an empirical monolith ('ea4all-automation-main-comp') toward a composable, lightweight operating pipeline. Trajectory is currently gated by governance prerequisites: establishing local ADR persistence and a localized capability inventory must precede substantive modularization.

docs.title: Capability Landscape
docs.text: Discovered capabilities encompass: - CI SDD Enforcement: Operational (High Confidence) - Forensic Codebase Discovery: Operational (High Confidence) - Local Runtime Capability Inventory: Absent (High Confidence) - Local Architecture Decision Scaffolding: Absent (High Confidence) - Modular Ingestion, Classification, & Synthesis Pipeline: Emerging / Proposed (Medium Confidence)

docs.title: Capability Dependencies
docs.text: The execution of downstream pipeline decomposition depends strictly upon the instantiation of local ADRs (governing module interface boundaries) and the creation of inventory.yaml (providing deterministic tracking of runtime entrypoints per ADR-038).

docs.title: Initiative Landscape
docs.text: Two key initiatives are active in the proposed phase: 1. 'Baseline Discovery': Encompasses inventory generation (aw-discovery-ea4all-automation-1) and core workflow boundary decomposition (aw-discovery-ea4all-automation-3). 2. 'Governance Foundation': Focuses on establishing the local ADR framework and decision scaffolding (aw-discovery-ea4all-automation-2).

docs.title: Governance State
docs.text: Governance readiness is assessed as 'needs_work'. While operational context rules (CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md) and CI workflows (cas-validate-sdd.yml) strictly enforce SDD specifications and testing standards, zero project-specific ADRs exist. Relying exclusively on inherited global CAS ADRs creates an alignment gap against the single-source-of-truth governance rule (ALIGN-001).

docs.title: Architecture State
docs.text: The system represents an Architecture Operating and Delivery Platform. Its observed structure consists of a single Python container ('ea4all-automation-core') with an entrypoint rooted in 'src/'. Architectural intent specifies a lightweight, three-stage composable architecture decoupling evidence intake, classification, and structured narrative synthesis.

docs.title: Intelligence State
docs.text: Intelligence capabilities remain in the conceptual design phase. The target vision specifies AI-assisted reasoning for evidence extraction, thematic synthesis, and pattern identification with mandatory human review guardrails. No autonomous runtime intelligence components are currently deployed in code.

docs.title: Operational State
docs.text: Operational tooling is structured around GitHub Actions CI enforcement (.github/workflows/cas-validate-sdd.yml) and automated pytest validation. Code modification protocols enforce surgical edits and specification compliance.
