docs.title: EA AUTOMATION VISION
docs.text:
Status: First working version Purpose: Define the intended direction for EA automation across personal, business, and architecture perspectives. This is a vision and set of design hypotheses, not a committed platform roadmap or claim of realised benefits.

VISION STATEMENT

EA Automation will make enterprise architecture practice more evidence-led, repeatable, and scalable while protecting the human judgement, accountability, and stakeholder engagement that give architecture its value.

It will turn proven elements of the EA operating model into reusable, governed workflows: from engagement intake and evidence handling through analysis, decision support, delivery enablement, and value follow-up. Automation will reduce avoidable effort and improve traceability; it will not automate consequential architectural accountability.

SOURCE-MATERIAL FOUNDATIONS

  • The EA operating model is problem-first, adaptive to the engagement, and connected from business intent to capability change, delivery, outcomes, and future evolution.
  • Evidence, uncertainty, trade-offs, decisions, and consequences should remain traceable.
  • Deterministic work should be automated deterministically where practical; AI should be used where synthesis, interpretation, or language work creates real leverage.
  • CAS is a reusable execution and governance substrate, rather than the public expression of every EA service.
  • The conceptual architecture blueprint is experimental. Its underlying hypotheses require validation through real delivery.

PERSONAL PERSPECTIVE

For the architect and EA practitioner, automation should create more time and attention for the work that requires professional judgement: understanding the real problem, challenging assumptions, resolving trade-offs, aligning stakeholders, and taking responsibility for recommendations.

The intended practitioner experience is a trusted working environment that:

  • makes required inputs, evidence gaps, assumptions, and decision points visible early;
  • converts repeatable preparation and production work into reliable, reviewable workflows;
  • provides structured intermediate artefacts rather than opaque AI-generated reports;
  • preserves provenance, so the architect can inspect and challenge how a conclusion was formed;
  • enables reuse of methods, patterns, and learning without forcing every engagement into a rigid template;
  • improves confidence and consistency while retaining the ability to adapt to the client context.

The central personal principle is: Automate execution where it creates leverage; preserve human attention for judgement, accountability, and high-value interaction.

BUSINESS PERSPECTIVE

EA Automation should enable the practice to deliver more consistent and valuable architecture work without scaling manual effort in direct proportion to demand.

The desired business outcomes are:

  • faster and more reliable conversion of engagement material into usable evidence, assessments, models, and decision support;
  • improved quality and consistency of EA deliverables, governance artefacts, and handover material;
  • stronger traceability from business intent through capability change, architectural direction, delivery evidence, and value measures;
  • reusable professional knowledge that can progressively become executable SOPs, Skills, and validated patterns;
  • more scalable architecture and advisory capacity while maintaining professional quality and client trust;
  • reduced dependency on document production as the primary measure of EA value;
  • a learning loop in which delivery evidence improves methods, automation candidates, and future engagements.

Success should be demonstrated through real-use measures, not assumed from technical capability alone. Initial measures should include time spent on repeatable delivery activities, evidence completeness, review rework, decision traceability, stakeholder usefulness, reuse frequency, and observed delivery or capability outcomes.

ARCHITECTURE PERSPECTIVE

EA Automation will be a composable, lightweight operating architecture rather than a single monolithic platform.

Its conceptual flow is:

Business and engagement context -> Evidence intake and classification -> Structured evidence, assumptions, gaps, and confidence -> Analysis, models, options, and decision support -> Human architectural review and judgement -> Client-facing artefacts, delivery guidance, and governance records -> Delivery and outcome evidence -> Learning, reuse, improvement, or retirement

The principal building blocks are:

  • SOPs and Skills: encode professional method, required inputs, decision criteria, constraints, quality criteria, and expected outputs.
  • Orchestration: selects the appropriate workflow, coordinates stages, records progress, and keeps execution lightweight.
  • Deterministic automation: performs parsing, extraction, normalisation, validation, calculations, consistency checks, rendering, packaging, and similar repeatable work.
  • AI-assisted reasoning: supports evidence extraction, thematic synthesis, pattern identification, option generation, audience-specific drafting, and analysis of large unstructured source sets.
  • Structured artefacts: hold evidence, assumptions, models, findings, decisions, risks, options, recommendations, and provenance before narrative is generated.
  • Governance and controls: provide decision rights, guardrails, validation, exception handling, auditability, and proportionate escalation.
  • Human oversight: owns material judgement, trade-offs, risk acceptance, consequential recommendations, stakeholder alignment, and final client-facing interpretation.

ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES

  • Start with a real delivery problem, not a technology opportunity.
  • Formulate a clear hypothesis before automating.
  • Build the smallest useful solution and validate it in real delivery.
  • Reuse before creating a new abstraction, framework, or tool.
  • Evidence before narrative.
  • Make uncertainty explicit; do not manufacture certainty from incomplete inputs.
  • Use AI as augmentation, not as unaccountable authority.
  • Keep human review mandatory for consequential judgement.
  • Prefer guardrails and actionable feedback over gatekeeping.
  • Make material decisions traceable from context and evidence to consequences.
  • Treat delivery as evidence that may refine architectural direction.
  • Learn, iterate, generalise, replace, or stop each automation based on demonstrated value.

SCOPE BOUNDARIES

This vision does not assume that every EA engagement needs the same depth of discovery, modelling, governance, delivery support, or automation. The workflow must be tailored to the decision, risk, complexity, evidence available, and intended outcome.

It also does not assume that every automation candidate merits a platform capability. A repeatable delivery problem must show sufficient frequency, effort, risk, or value before it is generalised.

FIRST DECISION

Use this vision as the decision frame for selecting EA automation experiments. The first candidates should be narrow, evidence-rich, repeatable activities with clear human review points, such as evidence intake, artefact consistency checks, structured assessment preparation, or traceable report assembly.

docs.title: EA AUTOMATION VISION
docs.text:
Status: First working version Purpose: Define the intended direction for EA automation across personal, business, and architecture perspectives. This is a vision and set of design hypotheses, not a committed platform roadmap or claim of realised benefits.

VISION STATEMENT

EA Automation will make enterprise architecture practice more evidence-led, repeatable, and scalable while protecting the human judgement, accountability, and stakeholder engagement that give architecture its value.

It will turn proven elements of the EA operating model into reusable, governed workflows: from engagement intake and evidence handling through analysis, decision support, delivery enablement, and value follow-up. Automation will reduce avoidable effort and improve traceability; it will not automate consequential architectural accountability.

SOURCE-MATERIAL FOUNDATIONS

  • The EA operating model is problem-first, adaptive to the engagement, and connected from business intent to capability change, delivery, outcomes, and future evolution.
  • Evidence, uncertainty, trade-offs, decisions, and consequences should remain traceable.
  • Deterministic work should be automated deterministically where practical; AI should be used where synthesis, interpretation, or language work creates real leverage.
  • CAS is a reusable execution and governance substrate, rather than the public expression of every EA service.
  • The conceptual architecture blueprint is experimental. Its underlying hypotheses require validation through real delivery.

PERSONAL PERSPECTIVE

For the architect and EA practitioner, automation should create more time and attention for the work that requires professional judgement: understanding the real problem, challenging assumptions, resolving trade-offs, aligning stakeholders, and taking responsibility for recommendations.

The intended practitioner experience is a trusted working environment that:

  • makes required inputs, evidence gaps, assumptions, and decision points visible early;
  • converts repeatable preparation and production work into reliable, reviewable workflows;
  • provides structured intermediate artefacts rather than opaque AI-generated reports;
  • preserves provenance, so the architect can inspect and challenge how a conclusion was formed;
  • enables reuse of methods, patterns, and learning without forcing every engagement into a rigid template;
  • improves confidence and consistency while retaining the ability to adapt to the client context.

The central personal principle is: Automate execution where it creates leverage; preserve human attention for judgement, accountability, and high-value interaction.

BUSINESS PERSPECTIVE

EA Automation should enable the practice to deliver more consistent and valuable architecture work without scaling manual effort in direct proportion to demand.

The desired business outcomes are:

  • faster and more reliable conversion of engagement material into usable evidence, assessments, models, and decision support;
  • improved quality and consistency of EA deliverables, governance artefacts, and handover material;
  • stronger traceability from business intent through capability change, architectural direction, delivery evidence, and value measures;
  • reusable professional knowledge that can progressively become executable SOPs, Skills, and validated patterns;
  • more scalable architecture and advisory capacity while maintaining professional quality and client trust;
  • reduced dependency on document production as the primary measure of EA value;
  • a learning loop in which delivery evidence improves methods, automation candidates, and future engagements.

Success should be demonstrated through real-use measures, not assumed from technical capability alone. Initial measures should include time spent on repeatable delivery activities, evidence completeness, review rework, decision traceability, stakeholder usefulness, reuse frequency, and observed delivery or capability outcomes.

ARCHITECTURE PERSPECTIVE

EA Automation will be a composable, lightweight operating architecture rather than a single monolithic platform.

Its conceptual flow is:

Business and engagement context -> Evidence intake and classification -> Structured evidence, assumptions, gaps, and confidence -> Analysis, models, options, and decision support -> Human architectural review and judgement -> Client-facing artefacts, delivery guidance, and governance records -> Delivery and outcome evidence -> Learning, reuse, improvement, or retirement

The principal building blocks are:

  • SOPs and Skills: encode professional method, required inputs, decision criteria, constraints, quality criteria, and expected outputs.
  • Orchestration: selects the appropriate workflow, coordinates stages, records progress, and keeps execution lightweight.
  • Deterministic automation: performs parsing, extraction, normalisation, validation, calculations, consistency checks, rendering, packaging, and similar repeatable work.
  • AI-assisted reasoning: supports evidence extraction, thematic synthesis, pattern identification, option generation, audience-specific drafting, and analysis of large unstructured source sets.
  • Structured artefacts: hold evidence, assumptions, models, findings, decisions, risks, options, recommendations, and provenance before narrative is generated.
  • Governance and controls: provide decision rights, guardrails, validation, exception handling, auditability, and proportionate escalation.
  • Human oversight: owns material judgement, trade-offs, risk acceptance, consequential recommendations, stakeholder alignment, and final client-facing interpretation.

ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES

  • Start with a real delivery problem, not a technology opportunity.
  • Formulate a clear hypothesis before automating.
  • Build the smallest useful solution and validate it in real delivery.
  • Reuse before creating a new abstraction, framework, or tool.
  • Evidence before narrative.
  • Make uncertainty explicit; do not manufacture certainty from incomplete inputs.
  • Use AI as augmentation, not as unaccountable authority.
  • Keep human review mandatory for consequential judgement.
  • Prefer guardrails and actionable feedback over gatekeeping.
  • Make material decisions traceable from context and evidence to consequences.
  • Treat delivery as evidence that may refine architectural direction.
  • Learn, iterate, generalise, replace, or stop each automation based on demonstrated value.

SCOPE BOUNDARIES

This vision does not assume that every EA engagement needs the same depth of discovery, modelling, governance, delivery support, or automation. The workflow must be tailored to the decision, risk, complexity, evidence available, and intended outcome.

It also does not assume that every automation candidate merits a platform capability. A repeatable delivery problem must show sufficient frequency, effort, risk, or value before it is generalised.

FIRST DECISION

Use this vision as the decision frame for selecting EA automation experiments. The first candidates should be narrow, evidence-rich, repeatable activities with clear human review points, such as evidence intake, artefact consistency checks, structured assessment preparation, or traceable report assembly.

Language model provider SDKs undergo rapid evolution and vary in invocation semantics. Decoupling agent reasoning logic from concrete model providers via a unified client abstraction pairing live router implementations with deterministic test doubles is required to avoid vendor lock-in and enable deterministic offline verification.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:

docs.title: Execution

docs.title: System Behaviour
docs.text: Eliminates vendor SDK coupling, standardizes token usage and error handling, and enables zero-cost deterministic offline execution for integration tests.

docs.title: Promotion Evidence
docs.text: Ratified Reference Architecture in ArchGov with verified implementations across LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient test doubles.

docs.title: Promotion Criteria
docs.text: Satisfied governance maturity and ratified reference architecture criteria.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Adopt the Provider-Agnostic LLM Facade as a mandatory architectural pattern across all CAS agent workflows and orchestration modules.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Source: governance-flow
  • Pattern: provider-agnostic-llm-facade
  • Promotion Recommendation: recommendation-provider-agnostic-llm-facade
  • Scope Classification: global
  • Scope Classification Artifact: pattern-scope-classification

Agentic systems often depend on closed model APIs or proprietary vendor SDKs. Switching providers or executing in offline CI/CD environments creates friction, vendor lock-in, and inconsistent error handling. The Provider-Agnostic LLM Facade encapsulates large language model invocations behind a cohesive interface (src/cas_runner/llm/base.py), isolating agent execution from vendor churn while providing symmetrical offline test doubles (MockLLMClient).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Applicability: Mandatory for all CAS components, agent steps, and workflow runners invoking large language models.

Applies across local development, offline CI/CD, and production multi-cloud deployments.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: Eliminates direct external SDK dependencies in domain and workflow logic. Enforces token budgeting, distributed tracing, and centralized review of model integrations.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text: Zero-overhead polymorphic dispatch via Python protocols. Dynamic routing across LiteLLM and hermetic mock test doubles for CI environments.

docs.title: System Behaviour
docs.text: Ensures deterministic fallback on API failures, normalized error handling, and centralized prompt/response caching.

docs.title: Promotion Evidence
docs.text:
• Recurring implementation across FlowRunner and AgenticMerger modules
  • Concrete AST symbols in src/cas_runner/llm/litellm_client.py (LiteLLMClient) and src/cas_runner/llm/mock_client.py (MockLLMClient)
  • Proven multi-provider test coverage across CI/CD environments
  • Governance model alignment with deterministic CI test doubles

docs.title: Promotion Criteria
docs.text: Significance, reusability, recurrence, evidence quality, governance maturity, and strategic alignment are fully met.

docs.title: Governance Risks
docs.text: Vendor abstraction leakage if vendor-specific parameters or proprietary prompt capabilities bypass the gateway contract.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Institutionalise Rule-Grounded Compliance Evaluation as a core global architectural pattern, evaluating codebase deltas against deterministic rule specifications rather than subjective LLM judgements.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Source: governance-flow
  • Pattern: rule-grounded-compliance-evaluation
  • Promotion Recommendation: recommendation-rule-grounded-compliance-evaluation
  • Scope Classification: global
  • Scope Classification Artifact: pattern-scope-classification

Autonomous and continuous architecture workflows require objective, machine-auditable verification of codebase deltas. Purely static linting lacks architectural intent awareness, while unconstrained LLM assessments suffer from hallucinations, non-determinism, and subjective drift. Codifying deterministic rules into ComplianceEngine provides repeatable, verifiable evaluation results across pipelines.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Applicability: All continuous delivery pipelines, pre-merge gate validations, and repository governance verification flows across organization workspaces.

Global organizational standard for continuous architectural compliance scanning and finding aggregation.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: Establishes deterministic compliance scoring and machine-readable findings as the authoritative gate for architecture evolution, removing ambiguity from promotion and review lifecycles.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text: Decouples delta analysis from subjective manual checks, executing rule validation within automated CI workflows and populating structured compliance metrics with zero LLM API dependency.

docs.title: System Behaviour
docs.text: Repository state mutations and candidate architectural changes produce repeatable pass/fail findings with explicit diagnostic reasons, preventing unauthorized deviations from organizational standards.

docs.title: Promotion Evidence
docs.text: Validated in src/cas_runner/governance/compliance_engine.py and verified across continuous architecture pipelines (cas-build-validation.yml, cas-continuous-architecture.yml) with production usage support.

docs.title: Promotion Criteria
docs.text: Satisfied all primary promotion criteria: significance, reusability, recurrence, evidence quality, governance maturity, and strategic alignment.

docs.title: Governance Risks
docs.text: Risk of rule inflation over time resulting in high maintenance overhead or contradictory compliance constraints, requiring periodic rule consolidation reviews.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Adopt Schema-Enforced Domain Contracts as a foundational architectural standard across all CAS pipeline boundaries and agent outputs.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Source: governance-flow
  • Pattern: schema-enforced-domain-contracts
  • Promotion Recommendation: recommendation-schema-enforced-domain-contracts
  • Scope Classification: global
  • Scope Classification Artifact: pattern-scope-classification

Schema-Enforced Domain Contracts establish strict data boundaries between non-deterministic actors (such as LLMs and autonomous agents) and core business state. By enforcing rigid Pydantic and JSON Schema validation prior to persistence or downstream propagation, the architecture guarantees system integrity, prevents state corruption, and enables deterministic pipeline execution.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Applicability: Mandatory for all agent task outputs, pipeline step boundaries, and persisted knowledge layer entities.

Enforces fail-fast validation before persistence across all CAS workflows.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: Guarantees system boundary and state integrity by strictly validating all agent and LLM outputs against rigid Pydantic schemas before persistence. Eliminates hallucinated attributes and structural payload corruption across pipeline stages.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text: Sub-millisecond validation overhead with Rust-backed Pydantic v2. Provides structured field-level diagnostics lowering MTTR during schema regressions.

docs.title: System Behaviour
docs.text: Guarantees that downstream workflow steps consume verified, strongly-typed domain entities without defensive null/type checks.

docs.title: Promotion Evidence
docs.text:
• Concrete AST symbols implemented in src/cas_runner/governance/models.py and src/cas_runner/steering/models.py
  • Enforced by build validation workflow gates and the ComplianceEngine
  • Validated across forensic diagnostic, AEM generator, and AID generation flows

docs.title: Promotion Criteria
docs.text: Significance, reusability, recurrence, evidence quality, governance maturity, and strategic alignment are fully met.

docs.title: Governance Risks
docs.text: Schema evolution friction across versioned artifacts; mitigated by explicit schema versioning and migration testing.

docs.text: Promote the Sequential Pipeline Flow Runner pattern to a core institutionalised global architectural standard, governing deterministic step execution and shared context propagation across continuous architecture steering flows.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Source: governance-flow
  • Pattern: sequential-pipeline-flow-runner
  • Promotion Recommendation: recommendation-sequential-pipeline-flow-runner
  • Scope Classification: global
  • Scope Classification Artifact: pattern-scope-classification

As autonomous agent workflows expand, unstructured multi-agent loops introduce non-deterministic execution, infinite loops, and debugging opacity. FlowRunner establishes a deterministic pipeline execution spine with shared context accumulation, termination on critical governance failure, and strict linear sequencing.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Applicability: Universal application across all continuous architecture steering workflows, command-line entrypoints, and multi-stage verification pipelines within ideas-to-life-cas and dependent systems.

Applicable globally across batch and CI/CD agent-driven architectural assessment and generation pipelines.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: Institutionalises deterministic stage progression and explicit gate checks, blocking unauthorized artifact mutation and guaranteeing auditable execution trails.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text: Standardises multi-phase step execution through FlowRunner, enabling early exit on validation failures and passing immutable contexts between pipeline components.

docs.title: System Behaviour
docs.text: Eliminates non-deterministic agent loop deviations and bounds token and compute expenditure by enforcing strictly ordered step chains.

docs.title: Promotion Evidence
docs.text: Implemented as the core FlowRunner orchestrator in src/cas_runner/runner.py, with declared step registries in src/cas_runner/steps/registry.py and entrypoint boundaries verified in CLI commands.

docs.title: Promotion Criteria
docs.text: Satisfied criteria include significance, reusability, recurrence, evidence quality, governance maturity, and strategic alignment.

docs.title: Governance Risks
docs.text: Pipeline latency accumulation across long sequential step chains, mitigated by selective short-circuiting and future DAG parallelism explorations.

Enforces distributed tracing and metric collection contracts across all agentic execution steps.

  • Business Intent and Code Intelligence remain purely theoretical with no implementation evidence.

docs.title: Evidence & Conclusions
docs.text:
• Repository contains a comprehensive set of foundational assets, including operational runbooks, agent guidance files, and extensive CAS skill/prompt definitions.
  • Governance templates (ADR, AEM, AID, AW) are well-defined but lack populated instances in the provided asset list, indicating a pre-execution or bootstrap state.
  • Orchestration flows and alignment engines are structurally ready but require actual architecture work and decision records to mature.
  • Knowledge layer templates enforce strict frontmatter and schema contracts, supporting deterministic derivation.

docs.title: Governance Maturity
docs.text: The project exhibits high foundational maturity with robust operational guidance, skill definitions, and prompt contracts. However, governance maturity is currently in the 'template-ready' phase. While the structural contracts for ADRs, AEMs, and AIDs are explicitly defined, there is an absence of actual governance evidence (populated ADRs, alignment reports, or executed architecture work logs) in the provided context. The system is prepared for governance but requires active execution to transition from design to operational maturity.

docs.title: Identified Gaps & Opportunities
docs.text:
• Absence of populated Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) and Architecture Work logs.
  • No live Architecture Evolution Map (AEM) or Architecture Intent Document (AID) instances present.
  • Governance workflow execution history is missing, making drift detection and alignment validation impossible at this stage.
  • Opportunity to bootstrap the first cycle of architecture work and alignment to establish the initial governance baseline.

docs.title: ❓ WHY: The Problem We Solve
docs.text: Architecture is traditionally static, written once, and quickly forgotten. Over time, the actual system diverges from the original design, leading to architecture decay, technical debt, and a disconnect between business requirements and the implemented code. With Coding Agents, this problem is exacerbated, as AI-generated code can introduce structural issues that are difficult to detect and correct.

docs.title: 💡 WHAT: The Value Proposition
docs.text: CAS is an Architecture Harness Platform. It replaces static documents with a living, continuously derived knowledge system. It prevents bad structure from being created in the first place through CAS Skills, and detects and corrects drift using automated workflows. It constantly measures the system's intended architecture against its actual implementation, with Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) serving as the Single Source of Truth (SSOT). It amplifies reuse and reduces cognitive load by providing a Knowledge Layer that is queryable, continuously updated, and accessible to both humans and AI agents.

docs.title: 👥 WHO: The Beneficiaries
docs.text:
• Execs: De-risks technology investments by guaranteeing alignment between spending (engineering effort) and business goals.
  • Architects & Engineers: Removes the burden of manual documentation while providing automated guardrails.
  • AI Ecosystem: Feeds crucial architectural context to autonomous coding agents, making AI-generated code safer and structurally sound.

docs.title: ⚙️ HOW: The Mechanism
docs.text:
CAS exposes a small set of composable flows, skills, and GitHub Actions. Each flow is a deterministic pipeline of steps that read from the knowledge layer and write back to it.

  • cas CLI is the user-facing surface that invokes those flows and adds lifecycle, observability, governance-state, and steering operations.
  • CI/CD pipelines and GitHub Actions invoke the same flows, enabling automated governance and steering of the system's architecture.

docs.title: E2E Steering Projection & Sync Sequence
docs.text:
This diagram illustrates the end-to-end flow of the CAS Steering Projection workflow, from indexing current system state to generating persona-specific LLM-augmented guidance and applying approved updates.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Host as CI / Developer CLI
    participant Runner as FlowRunner
    participant Step as SteeringProjectionStep
    participant Core as Deterministic Engines
    participant Synth as ArchitectureSynthesizer
    participant LLM as LLM (Reasoning Contract)
    participant Rend as ManagedSectionRenderer
    participant Proj as SteeringPatchProjector
    participant Apply as ManagedSectionApplier

    Host->>Runner: cas run steering-projection-flow
    Runner->>Step: execute()

    Note over Step, Core: Phase 1: Deterministic Extraction
    Step->>Core: build_index() [Indexer]
    Step->>Core: analyze(baseline) [Analyzer]
    Step->>Core: extract(deltas) [Extractor]
    Core-->>Step: current_deltas, capabilities

    Note over Step, LLM: Phase 2: Persona-Driven Synthesis
    Step->>Core: scan() [ArtifactScanner]
    Core-->>Step: artifact_claims (markers)
    Step->>Synth: synthesize(request)

    par Parallel Synthesis (README, AGENTS, Platform)
        Synth->>LLM: reason(synthesis-narrative)
        Synth->>LLM: reason(synthesis-rules)
        Synth->>LLM: reason(synthesis-context)
    end
    LLM-->>Synth: synthesized_markdown (JSON)
    Synth-->>Step: synthesized_content_map

    Note over Step, Proj: Phase 3: Projection Bundling
    Step->>Rend: render(project, deltas, capabilities, synth_content)
    Rend-->>Step: managed_section_proposals
    Step->>Proj: persist(project, index, findings, proposals)
    Proj-->>Step: SteeringProjectionBundle (.md)

    Step-->>Runner: bundle_output
    Runner-->>Host: Done. Projection Persisted.

    Note over Host, Apply: Optional Approval Step

    Host->>Apply: cas steering apply --projection <id>
    Apply->>Apply: plan(proposals) [Validation & Diffs]
    Apply->>Apply: apply(plan) [Atomic Surgical Injection]
    Apply-->>Host: Steering Artifacts Updated

docs.title: Flow Description
docs.text:
1. Extraction: The workflow begins by deterministically indexing the current project state and comparing it against a baseline (e.g., previous projection) to extract architectural deltas and capabilities.
  2. Synthesis: The ArchitectureSynthesizer identifies existing managed markers in steering artifacts. It dispatches concurrent requests to the LLM via the unified reasoning contract, providing persona-specific prompts and current content to ensure high-signal, incremental updates.
  3. Bundling: The ManagedSectionRenderer prioritizes synthesized content over raw data tables. The SteeringPatchProjector then persists a human-readable projection bundle containing all proposed changes.
  4. Application: Once the projection is reviewed (manually or via CI), the ManagedSectionApplier performs a surgical, atomic update, injecting the new content strictly between the <!-- CAS-STEERING --> markers.

docs.title: Patterns Illustrated
docs.text:
• Deterministic Core / Selective Augmentation: Core state extraction is deterministic; LLM is used only to improve guidance signal.
  • Persona-Driven Synthesis: Content is tailored for specific audiences (Humans vs. Agents).
  • Safe Surgical Injection: Updates are limited to managed markers to prevent data loss in human-authored sections.

docs.title: ❓ WHY: The Problem We Solve
docs.text: Architecture is traditionally static, written once, and quickly forgotten. Over time, the actual system diverges from the original design, leading to architecture decay, technical debt, and a disconnect between business requirements and the implemented code. With Coding Agents, this problem is exacerbated, as AI-generated code can introduce structural issues that are difficult to detect and correct.

docs.title: 💡 WHAT: The Value Proposition
docs.text: CAS is an Architecture Harness Platform. It replaces static documents with a living, continuously derived knowledge system. It prevents bad structure from being created in the first place through CAS Skills, and detects and corrects drift using automated workflows. It constantly measures the system's intended architecture against its actual implementation, with Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) serving as the Single Source of Truth (SSOT). It amplifies reuse and reduces cognitive load by providing a Knowledge Layer that is queryable, continuously updated, and accessible to both humans and AI agents.

docs.title: 👥 WHO: The Beneficiaries
docs.text:
• Execs: De-risks technology investments by guaranteeing alignment between spending (engineering effort) and business goals.
  • Architects & Engineers: Removes the burden of manual documentation while providing automated guardrails.
  • AI Ecosystem: Feeds crucial architectural context to autonomous coding agents, making AI-generated code safer and structurally sound.

docs.title: ⚙️ HOW: The Mechanism
docs.text:
CAS exposes a small set of composable flows, skills, and GitHub Actions. Each flow is a deterministic pipeline of steps that read from the knowledge layer and write back to it.

  • cas CLI is the user-facing surface that invokes those flows and adds lifecycle, observability, governance-state, and steering operations.
  • CI/CD pipelines and GitHub Actions invoke the same flows, enabling automated governance and steering of the system's architecture.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: Separate orchestration, reasoning, and knowledge access responsibilities through explicit contracts to enable implementation-agnostic workflow execution.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The CAS framework requires a clear separation between the orchestration layer (Runner), reasoning logic (Workflows), and data access layer (Knowledge Providers). This separation is essential for systems adopting the CAS workflow model to ensure modularity and portability across different execution environments.

docs.title: Agentic Profile
docs.text: The CAS Runner orchestrates execution and validates compliance, while Workflows encapsulate reasoning logic and Knowledge Providers supply context. Agents must adhere to prompt-based contracts to maintain decoupling.

docs.title: Forces
docs.text: The pattern balances portability, modularity, and governance requirements through explicit contracts.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
• Portability across execution environments
  • Modular evolution of reasoning capabilities
  • Implementation-agnostic workflow design

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Strict separation of reasoning logic from orchestration runners
  • Prompt-based contracts for data access abstraction

docs.title: Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Additional contract management overhead
  • Potential latency from abstraction layers

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Implement a decoupled execution model where the CAS Runner handles orchestration and validation, Workflows contain pure reasoning logic, and Knowledge Providers abstract data access. Communication between layers is enforced via prompt-based contracts, ensuring that reasoning logic remains independent of storage and execution infrastructure.

docs.title: Operationalisation
docs.text: Adopting this pattern requires restructuring workflow implementations to enforce layer separation and integrating automated validation into the CI/CD pipeline.

docs.title: Workflow Implications
docs.text:
• Refactor existing workflows to isolate reasoning logic from orchestration calls
  • Define and version prompt-based contracts for Knowledge Provider interactions
  • Update onboarding specifications to reference the decoupled execution model

docs.title: Automation Opportunities
docs.text:
• Implement CI/CD validation to detect violations of the decoupled execution model
  • Automate compliance checks through architecture alignment reviews
  • Generate runtime-native AW artifacts to monitor pattern adherence

docs.title: Implementation Signals
docs.text: Signals include the presence of distinct Runner, Workflow, and Knowledge Provider components, explicit prompt-based contracts between layers, and CI/CD guardrails enforcing decoupling.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: High confidence based on recurring architecture work, current state support, and cross-project applicability.

docs.title: Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The CI-Driven Steering Projection pattern synchronizes evolving repository facts into actionable prompt context and steering models for autonomous developer agents. By anchoring synchronization directly within continuous integration workflows, architectural facts derived from Git deltas are compiled deterministically and projected into downstream developer prompts and documentation without running continuous background daemons.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• Codebases where developer agent prompts or architectural context drift rapidly from the underlying implementation.
  • Multi-contributor engineering teams requiring synchronized steering documentation without imposing manual governance overhead on every PR.
  • Environments requiring strict governance boundaries where architecture projections must be proposed via pull requests rather than destructive direct mutations.
  • Organizations seeking to optimize developer tool costs by utilizing ephemeral CI compute over 24/7 background agent services.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• Monolithic repositories without automated CI pipelines or with severe CI runner resource constraints.
  • Ultra-low latency interactive coding workflows where developers require instant cross-workspace feedback in sub-second intervals.
  • Unstructured or prototype codebases lacking defined module boundaries, AST stability, or architectural conventions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    gitTrigger["Git Event Trigger (External System)"]
    ciRunner["CI Projection Runner (Container)"]
    factExtractor["Delta Fact Extractor (Container)"]
    steeringGen["Steering Model Compiler (Container)"]
    repoStore[("Repository Workspace (Data store)")]
    proposalOut["Steering Proposal PR (Container)"]

    gitTrigger -->|1. Push / PR Event| ciRunner
    ciRunner -->|2. Compute Git Diffs| factExtractor
    factExtractor -->|3. Query Code and AST| repoStore
    factExtractor -->|4. Verified Fact Tuples| steeringGen
    steeringGen -->|5. Compile Context and Prompts| proposalOut
    proposalOut -->|6. Safe Mutation Proposal| repoStore

    classDef container fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef store fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef external fill:#666666,stroke:#333333,color:#fff
    class ciRunner,factExtractor,steeringGen,proposalOut container
    class repoStore store
    class gitTrigger external

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• CI Projection Runner (.github/workflows/cas-build-steering-projection.yml): Orchestrates execution triggers on repository events, provides ephemeral isolation, and manages permission scopes for projection generation.
  • Continuous Architecture Pipeline (.github/workflows/cas-continuous-architecture.yml): Triggers architectural analysis, governance validation, and boundary verification across active pull requests.
  • Steering Projection Engine (steering/models.py): Defines domain structures, validates architectural delta facts, and renders machine-readable prompt additions for local developer agents.
  • Delta Fact Extractor (steering/extractors.py): Analyzes Git diffs, AST structures, and metadata deltas between commits to extract immutable architectural facts.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
• Continuous Integration Environment: GitHub Actions was selected for deep integration with repository lifecycle events, secret management, and ephemeral runtime isolation.
  • Deterministic Delta Extraction: Python standard AST libraries combined with Git plumbing commands provide fast, deterministic discovery of boundary shifts.
  • Schema-Enforced Modeling: Pydantic models in steering/models.py guarantee structural integrity before publishing prompt facts.
  • Alternatives Set Aside: Continuous indexing background daemons were rejected due to idle operational costs, high failure surface area, and branch desynchronization risks. Direct commit strategies were rejected to prevent bypass of peer review controls.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Proposal Pull-Request Variant: Automatically submits a governance pull request with compiled markdown facts and steering updates whenever architectural changes exceed predefined drift metrics.
  • Ephemeral Artifact Packaging: Generates localized context bundles uploaded as CI artifacts, consumed directly by developer IDE plugins without branch pollution.
  • Pre-Merge Enforcement Variant: Operates as a required status check that validates developer additions against known steering contracts, failing the build on invariant breaches.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Employs deterministic parsing and pinned Git references to ensure projection generation is idempotent and reproducible across environments.
  • Performance & Latency: Focuses solely on commit deltas rather than complete repository re-indexes, completing pipeline stages in under 60 seconds.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Eliminates dedicated agent server infrastructure by executing purely on on-demand CI build allocations.
  • Operability: Emits standard GitHub status outputs, step summaries, and structured diffs accessible directly within the pull request experience.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Direct Branch Mutation: Allowing the CI workflow to push changes directly into trunk branches. Remedy: Enforce branch protection rules and route all projection updates through pull-request proposals.
  • Prompt Context Bloat: Over-indexing irrelevant internal implementation details into agent prompt bundles, leading to developer fatigue and agent distraction. Remedy: Restrict steering projections to structural boundaries, exported interfaces, and explicit architectural facts.
  • Stochastic Ingestion: Relying on generative models to determine baseline architectural changes. Remedy: Ground fact extraction in deterministic AST parsers and structured Git diff tools.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
1. Baseline Ingestion: Introduce the extraction scripts into existing CI pipelines to build steering projection artifacts on push events.
  2. Review Integration: Enable the proposal pull-request mechanism with designated CODEOWNERS reviews to validate proposed architectural steering updates.
  3. Agent Consumption: Point local developer agents and prompt orchestrators to the compiled steering projections.
  4. Governance Ownership: Enterprise Architecture & Developer Experience teams.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Declarative Agent Command Registry
Reference Architecture: Declarative Agent Command Registry
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Declarative Agent Command Registry pattern externalizes agent task specifications, operational interfaces, and skills into version-controlled declarative manifests (such as TOML files) within the repository. It creates a standardized, decoupled contract between autonomous agents, human engineers, and runtime tool execution harnesses.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When coordinating multi-agent workflows where agents and human engineers must discover, parameterize, and invoke identical architectural skills (such as planning, analysis, specification, and migration).
  • When decoupling agent capability definitions from hardcoded runner scripts, command-line interfaces, or proprietary orchestrator code.
  • When building project-extensible toolsets where individual repositories or domain teams need to customize command arguments, prompt contexts, or execution environments without modifying global tooling binaries.
  • When enterprise governance requires auditability, linting, and semantic versioning of all agent-executable operations.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• In simple single-agent setups or monolithic scripts where commands are static, non-extensible, and have no multi-agent or multi-environment handoffs.
  • For high-frequency, millisecond-critical synchronous micro-routines where parsing declarative manifests on every invocation introduces unacceptable overhead.
  • Where command payloads require complex imperative logic that cannot be expressed cleanly as declarative contract specifications with modular execution bindings.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Dev["Developer / Human Operator (User)"]
    Agent["Autonomous AI Agent (Container)"]
    CLI["Command Line Dispatcher (Container)"]
    Registry[("Command Registry Manifests (.agents/commands/*.toml) (Data store)")]
    Executor["Skill Execution Runtime (Container)"]
    Target["Target Project / System (External System)"]

    Dev -->|1. Invokes skill command| CLI
    Agent -->|1. Dispatches sub-task| CLI
    CLI -->|2. Discovers and validates manifests| Registry
    CLI -->|3. Resolves contract & invokes| Executor
    Executor -->|4. Executes operations against| Target

    classDef container fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef store fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef external fill:#666666,stroke:#333333,color:#fff
    class Dev,Agent,CLI,Executor container
    class Registry store
    class Target external

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Command Registry Manifests (.agents/commands/*.toml): Provides human-readable, schema-validated declarative configurations defining skill metadata, input arguments, default prompt templates, and execution prerequisites.
  • Command Line Dispatcher (cli/dispatcher): Discovers manifest definitions across standard paths, parses configuration trees, performs argument validation, and provides identical invocation semantics to humans and agents.
  • Skill Execution Runtime (runtime/executor): Injects validated parameters into prompt templates, manages execution context, coordinates model calls or external tool execution, and returns structured command results.
  • Registry Schema Validator (tools/validators/command_schema): Performs CI/CD and pre-commit schema validation against command manifests to guarantee backward compatibility and parameter integrity.

docs.title: Selected Standards & Technologies
docs.text:
• TOML (Tom's Obvious Minimal Language): Selected for manifest definitions over JSON and YAML due to strict typing, native multiline string support for prompt templates, support for comments, and high human readability.
  • Pydantic / JSON Schema: Selected for defining and enforcing the specification contract of the TOML files, enabling pre-execution validation and automated documentation synthesis.
  • Git-based Repository Versioning: Selected as the authoritative registry store, ensuring commands are co-located, versioned, and branched alongside the codebase they operate on.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered & Set Aside
docs.text:
• YAML Manifests: Set aside due to parsing ambiguities, silent type-coercion bugs, and indentation sensitivity in long prompts.
  • Centralized Database / Service Registry: Rejected for command definitions to avoid distributed synchronization overhead, network partitioning failure modes, and detachment from repository-specific code versions.
  • Hardcoded CLI Flags / Procedural Handlers: Set aside because they create tight coupling between agent frameworks and CLI code, preventing project-level customization of agent skills.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Variant A: In-Repo Scoped Registry (Default): Command manifests are stored directly within the repository under .agents/commands/. All agents and developers operate on the version locked to the current Git commit.
  • Variant B: Federated Shared Command Registry: Manifests are distributed as versioned packages or Git submodules, allowing cross-project sharing of standardized commands with local project overrides.
  • Variant C: Dynamic Agent-Synthesized Registry: Autonomous agents dynamically propose or instantiate temporary command manifests for complex decomposed workflows, validating them against the central schema prior to execution.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Manifests are evaluated locally without remote network lookups, eliminating network partitions during agent execution. Schema validation prevents malformed commands or missing arguments from executing.
  • Performance & Latency: Manifest discovery and TOML deserialization add negligible latency (<15ms overhead per invocation). In-memory caching minimizes disk I/O.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Compact declarative manifests reduce token bloat by exposing structured command interfaces rather than passing raw multi-thousand-token prompt definitions across multi-agent contexts.
  • Operability & Governance: Every command addition or modification is tracked through Git history, code reviews, and automated CI pull request checks.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Anti-Pattern 1: Inlining Complex Executable Code in Manifests: Embedding raw scripts inside TOML command manifests turns declarative contracts into hard-to-test script dumping grounds. Remedy: Keep manifests purely declarative; point execution attributes to dedicated, unit-tested script files or container entrypoints.
  • Anti-Pattern 2: Divergent Human and Agent Invocation Schemas: Creating a CLI command interface for developers while providing agents an alternative, out-of-band JSON API to perform the same actions. Remedy: Route both human CLI calls and agent tool dispatches through the single declarative registry entrypoint.
  • Anti-Pattern 3: Unversioned Breaking Schema Changes: Renaming required arguments in manifests without backward compatibility, breaking automated pipelines. Remedy: Follow semantic versioning for command manifests and run schema-compatibility linters in CI pipelines.

docs.title: Migration Path
docs.text:
1. Standardize Directory Structure: Create .agents/commands/ in the root repository.
  2. Extract Core Commands: Migrate existing hardcoded agent or CLI commands (e.g., plan, analyze) into TOML manifests such as speckit.plan.toml and speckit.analyze.toml.
  3. Implement Runner Validation: Update the command dispatcher to read and validate inputs against the declarative manifest prior to execution.
  4. Adopt CI Enforcement: Integrate schema linting into pull-request checks to ensure all .toml files adhere to the canonical schema.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Deterministic Mock Evaluation Harness
Reference Architecture: Deterministic Mock Evaluation Harness
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Deterministic Mock Evaluation Harness provides a drop-in, hermetic test double for language model clients and external agent dependencies. It guarantees predictable, zero-cost, and low-latency evaluation of orchestration pipelines, schema parsers, and governance decision gates.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• Automated CI/CD pipelines executing unit, integration, or regression suites against agent workflows.
  • Schema validation and structural parsing tests where prompt/response variations need exact matching without external network variance.
  • Cost-sensitive developer test loops requiring instant feedback cycles without incurring LLM token costs or rate limits.
  • Testing edge cases, deterministic error handling, and timeout behavior that are difficult to trigger reliably with live upstream APIs.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• End-to-end model quality, accuracy, hallucination, or benchmark evaluations where true non-deterministic model reasoning is being measured.
  • Real-world prompt engineering validation requiring true model emergent responses.
  • Final pre-production canary or smoke testing against live provider endpoints to verify credentials, API version parity, and dynamic network routing.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    testRunner["Test Runner / CI Pipeline (Container)"]
    agentCore["Agent Pipeline / CAS Runner (Container)"]
    mockLLM["Mock LLM Client (Container)"]
    fixtureStore[("Fixture / Response Catalog (Data store)")]
    liveProvider["External LLM Provider (External System)"]

    testRunner -->|1. Executes test suite| agentCore
    agentCore -->|2. Dispatches prompt / messages| mockLLM
    mockLLM -->|3. Resolves pre-recorded response| fixtureStore
    mockLLM -.->|Bypassed in CI| liveProvider

    classDef container fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef store fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef external fill:#666666,stroke:#333333,color:#fff
    class testRunner,agentCore,mockLLM container
    class fixtureStore store
    class liveProvider external

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Mock LLM Client (src/cas_runner/llm/mock_client.py): Implements standard LLM interface contracts, matching prompts and intents to deterministic fixtures or programmatic responses without external network I/O.
  • Agent Runner / Pipeline Engine (src/cas_runner/runner.py): Orchestrates multi-step reasoning, tool invocations, and state transitions, operating agnostic of whether the underlying client is live or mocked.
  • Fixture Response Catalog (tests/fixtures/llm_responses/): Stores deterministic structured payloads, tool calls, and error frames indexed by prompt hashes, message sequences, or semantic scenario keys.
  • CI Test Runner (.github/workflows/ci.yml): Automates test suite execution in hermetic CI/CD environments, asserting pipeline correctness, state transitions, and contract adherence.

docs.title: Recommended Choices
docs.text:
• In-Memory Interface Substitution: Python Protocol or ABC interface implementation substituted at runtime via dependency injection.
  • Fixture Formats: Schema-validated JSON/YAML payloads conforming to provider response specifications.

docs.title: Alternatives Set Aside
docs.text:
• Network Replay Proxies (VCR.py / Polly.js): Set aside due to brittle serialization when managing streaming chunks and subtle protocol-level coupling.
  • Local Containerized LLMs (Ollama / Llama.cpp): Set aside due to heavy runner resource footprints, unpredictable execution times, and compute costs.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Static Exact Matching: Returns static responses mapped to exact prompt strings or cryptographic hashes of normalized prompts.
  • Dynamic Rule-Based Synthesis: Inspects incoming request schemas and synthesizes conforming mock arguments programmatically.
  • Sequential Turn Playbook: Replays ordered sequences of responses to simulate multi-turn dialogues and state-dependent agent deliberations.
  • Fault Injection Double: Programmatically simulates upstream provider failure modes, including HTTP 429 rate limits, context window overflow exceptions, and malformed JSON payloads.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Eliminates 100% of test flakiness caused by upstream provider outages, API throttling, token rate limits, and model non-determinism.
  • Performance & Latency: Generates responses in sub-millisecond durations (<5ms), reducing multi-minute regression suites to seconds.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Zero token cost incurred during local development loops and CI/CD pull request validation runs.
  • Operability: Zero credential or API key requirements for CI runners or onboarding developers; fails fast with explicit unmatched prompt errors.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Contract Drift / Provider Divergence: Allowing mock responses to drift from true upstream API response shapes over time. Remedy: Implement automated provider contract tests that run on a scheduled cadence against live endpoints.
  • Over-Mocking Runner Logic: Embedding complex decision branches inside the mock client rather than testing the runner's handling logic. Remedy: Keep mock client logic minimal, focusing on simple mapping and fixture playback.
  • Permissive Unmatched Fallbacks: Returning default empty responses when encountering unexpected prompts. Remedy: Throw strict assertion exceptions whenever an unmapped prompt is passed to the mock.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
• Starting Points: Define an interface abstraction across all agent execution code; introduce MockLLMClient implementing that interface in test suites.
  • Migration Path: Identify existing unit and integration tests executing real LLM API calls; capture actual response payloads into structured fixture files; swap provider injection to MockLLMClient.
  • Governance & Ownership: Owned by Core Platform and Architecture teams. Teams adopting the pattern must participate in contract validation pipelines to prevent mock obsolescence.

docs.title: Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The File-Backed Blackboard Workspace pattern utilizes a version-controlled, hierarchical filesystem structure as a shared blackboard for multi-agent systems, automated workflows, and human engineering teams. It allows independent modules and agents to exchange state, preserve intermediate artifacts, and maintain complete provenance without provisioning external database backends.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• Multi-agent or multi-step execution pipelines where decoupled agents or tools need to inspect, append, and mutate state asynchronously.
  • Workflows that require complete auditability, provenance, and deterministic state reproduction tied directly to Git commit SHA revisions.
  • Continuous Integration (CI) and local developer environments requiring identical execution context without provisioning external backing stores (e.g., PostgreSQL, Redis).
  • Collaborative human-in-the-loop workflows where pull requests and code reviews gate changes to system templates, global rules, and execution profiles.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• Ultra-high-throughput transactional workloads requiring sub-millisecond ACID updates across dozens of concurrent writers.
  • Systems with high-frequency concurrent mutating writes that would trigger severe Git merge contention or lock churn.
  • Large binary artifact storage or streaming datasets exceeding tens of gigabytes, which bloat repository trees (object storage like S3/GCS is preferred for payload blobs).
  • Workloads requiring dynamic ad-hoc relational querying, complex joins, or graph traversals across runtime entities.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Workspace Scaffolder / Bootstrapper (src/cas_runner/bootstrap.py): Responsible for constructing standard blackboard folder structures (cas-knowledge/global, cas-knowledge/projects, cas-knowledge/runtime, cas-knowledge/templates) and merging governance blocks.
  • Local Knowledge Provider (src/cas_runner/knowledge/provider.py): Implements access controls, structured serialization (YAML/JSON), and schema validations, shielding agents from low-level filesystem I/O.
  • Runtime Blackboard (cas-knowledge/runtime/): Transient execution space storing execution-profile.yaml, execution traces, and agent communication logs for the active pipeline run.
  • Governance and Template Catalog (cas-knowledge/global/, cas-knowledge/templates/): Canonical repository of immutable reference guidelines, evaluation constraints, and standardized agent prompts.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
• File Formats: YAML and Markdown with YAML frontmatter for human readability, ease of diffing, and compatibility with LLM prompt windows.
  • Storage Engine: POSIX filesystem backed by Git version control, enabling time-travel debugging and native branching/merging.
  • Atomic Write Semantics: Tempfile creation followed by atomic replacement (os.replace) to prevent read corruptions during concurrent agent reads.
  • Alternatives Set Aside:
  • Redis / Key-Value Stores: Added infrastructure footprint without branch/commit traceability.
  • Relational Databases (PostgreSQL/MySQL): Hard to diff in Git PR workflows and prohibitive for lightweight standalone CLI/CI runs.
  • SQLite: Lacks git-diff transparency and causes merge conflict resolution challenges when checked into source control.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Local Ephemeral Workspace: Used in local test suites and isolated worker nodes where output files are discarded post-execution.
  • PR-Gated Persistent Blackboard: Long-lived multi-agent coordination where changes are written to dedicated branch workspaces and merged via automated pull requests.
  • Hybrid Content-Addressable Workspace: Metadata and structured control files reside in Git, while large payloads and model outputs are written to S3 with content hashes stored in blackboard files.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Eliminates external network database dependencies; filesystem guarantees crash resilience when combined with atomic write operations.
  • Performance & Latency: Sub-millisecond reads for local configuration files; latency scales with disk I/O.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Zero cost beyond basic disk utilization; no recurring database server hosting or license expenses.
  • Operability: Highly maintainable using familiar developer tooling (git log, diff, jq, yq).

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Shared Direct Appends: Agents concurrently writing to the same file without unique identifiers. Remedy: Segregate state by task ID or execution step.
  • Git Repository Bloat: Storing binary outputs or model checkpoints in the blackboard repository. Remedy: Use Git LFS or external object storage with URI references.
  • Unvalidated Schema Drift: Uncontrolled file schemas that break downstream parsing. Remedy: Enforce Pydantic or JSON schema validation at the Knowledge Provider boundary.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
1. Scaffold Structure: Run the workspace bootstrap routine to instantiate standard directories (global/, projects/, runtime/, templates/).
  2. Encapsulate Access: Restrict file read/write operations to the LocalKnowledgeProvider interface.
  3. CI Validation: Add pre-commit or CI hooks that validate YAML schemas and guard against large binary commits.
  4. Governance: Managed under Domain core-platform-governance, Initiative autonomous-agent-foundations.

docs.title: Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The File-Backed Knowledge Repository pattern establishes a decentralized, transparent, and auditable blackboard architecture by persisting architectural, operational, and governance artifacts directly as structured files (Markdown, YAML, JSON) inside standard Git repositories.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When distributed software agents and human engineers must collaborate, peer-review, and evolve architectural designs, decisions (ADRs), and compliance policies using familiar pull-request workflows.
  • When governance, configuration, and architectural metadata need cryptographically verifiable version history, branching, and atomic commit semantics without introducing external database dependencies.
  • When bootstrapping developer tools, CLIs, or localized runtime runners that must function offline or in air-gapped CI/CD environments with zero relational database friction.
  • When artifacts must be human-readable, portable across disparate operating platforms, and immune to proprietary database vendor lock-in.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• When data access patterns demand high-frequency, millisecond-latency concurrent transactional updates (ACID transaction volume > 50 writes/sec), which would cause extreme Git merge conflicts and lock contention.
  • When datasets contain sensitive runtime secrets, highly dynamic telemetry streams, or high-volume ephemeral session state.
  • When deep relational graph querying, multi-table joins, or sub-millisecond full-text indexed searches across millions of entities are required without an intermediary indexing cache.

docs.text:

  • Workspace Bootstrapper (src/cas_runner/bootstrap.py): Provides deterministic scaffolding, template extraction, and initialization of local workspace governance files against centralized reference definitions.
  • Governance Block Merge Engine (src/cas_runner/bootstrap.py:merge_cas_governance_block): Performs idempotent updates, schema preservation, and block-level reconciliation between active workspace definitions and upstream template specifications.
  • Audit and Schema Verifier (.github/workflows/knowledge-audit.yml): Continuous integration verification layer that enforces structural schema constraints and linting on committed repository artifacts.

docs.title: Adopted Technologies
docs.text:
• Git Version Control: Native versioning engine providing immutability, cryptographic commit hashing, peer-review branching models, and decentralized synchronization without database infrastructure.
  • Structured Serialization (YAML, JSON, Frontmatter Markdown): Balances human readability with strict machine parsability via standard JSON Schema and Pydantic models.
  • Python (Standard Library & PyYAML): Lightweight bootstrapping and synchronization scripts without heavy external ORM or database client dependencies.

docs.title: Considered & Set Aside
docs.text:
• Relational Databases (PostgreSQL): Rejected due to infrastructure deployment overhead, lack of native decentralized branching, and friction in developer PR review cycles.
  • Headless CMS / NoSQL (MongoDB, Contentful): Rejected to prevent vendor lock-in, recurring operational hosting costs, and network-boundary dependencies during local developer execution.
  • Wiki Systems (Confluence): Rejected due to weak schema validation, lack of programmatic API parity with developer IDEs, and absence of branch-merge auditability.

docs.title: 1. In-Repo Colocated Knowledge Store
docs.text: Knowledge artifacts reside directly within the application codebase (./knowledge/ or ./cas-knowledge/). Best suited for single-repository systems where code changes and architectural updates must be committed atomically in the same pull request.

docs.title: 2. Centralized Multi-Repo Knowledge Hub
docs.text: A standalone Git repository acts as an enterprise-wide blackboard. Downstream application repositories mount or synchronize templates via Git subtrees, submodules, or CLI synchronization utilities (cas_runner/bootstrap.py).

docs.title: 3. Read-Through Memory-Cached Repository
docs.text: Runtime services clone the Git repository into an in-memory or localized RocksDB/SQLite index at startup. Read operations bypass disk parsing while writes persist back through standard Git commit workflows.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
• Highly resilient to data loss due to decentralized distributed replication inherent to Git.
  • Every checkout functions as a complete snapshot backup. Fault recovery involves simple commit checkouts or branch restores.

docs.title: Performance & Latency
docs.text:
• Read Latency: Sub-millisecond localized disk I/O when read directly from SSD storage or cached into memory.
  • Write Latency: Higher latency (100ms - 2000ms) during Git commit, rebase, and push operations; acceptable for governance events but unsuited for high-throughput transactional logging.

docs.title: Cost & Efficiency
docs.text:
• Near-zero recurring infrastructure operational costs. Relies on commodity cloud repository hosting (GitHub, GitLab) or local developer file systems.
  • Eliminates the need for managed database instances, continuous database patching, and persistent connection pool management.

docs.title: Operability & Governance
docs.text:
• Native operational visibility using standard Git tools (git log, git diff, git blame).
  • Full cryptographic provenance and change ownership tracked across all governance artifacts.

docs.title: 1. The High-Frequency Transaction Log Pitfall
docs.text:
• Anti-pattern: Attempting to record real-time agent execution telemetry or per-event logs as separate Git commits.
  • Pitfall: Git object databases inflate rapidly, creating lock contention (index.lock) and merge collisions.
  • Remedy: Stream operational telemetry to disk-based JSON Lines files excluded by .gitignore or forward to external log aggregators; retain Git strictly for milestone state and governance declarations.

docs.title: 2. Free-Form Unstructured Documentation
docs.text:
• Anti-pattern: Writing arbitrary, unvalidated markdown files without consistent metadata schemas.
  • Pitfall: Downstream tools and automated agent pipelines fail to parse disparate architectural assertions.
  • Remedy: Enforce JSON schema validation over YAML frontmatter in CI gates before commits are merged.

docs.title: 3. Unresolved Concurrent Merge Contention
docs.text:
• Anti-pattern: Multiple distributed runners writing simultaneously to a single shared remote tracking branch without locking or automated rebasing.
  • Pitfall: Push rejections and fractured commit histories.
  • Remedy: Implement isolated working branches per agent run or use idempotent block-merging logic as provided in merge_cas_governance_block.

docs.text:
1. Establish a root cas-knowledge/ directory in the repository to store architectural decisions, pattern catalogs, and team conventions.
  2. Adopt the workspace bootstrap utility (src/cas_runner/bootstrap.py) to scaffold initial configuration files and register local project templates.
  3. Integrate schema validation in pre-commit hooks or continuous integration pipelines to lint JSON/YAML frontmatter.

  • Phase 2: Introduce automated CLI utilities (cas-runner) to parse repository artifacts during local build and test execution.
  • Phase 3: Connect CI validation workflows to verify that architectural specifications align with codebase implementations.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: File-System Structured Knowledge Repository
Reference Architecture: File-System Structured Knowledge Repository
Purpose
docs.text: The File-System Structured Knowledge Repository pattern establishes an organized, version-controlled hierarchy of flat files (Markdown, YAML, and JSON) directly within source control as the authoritative architectural source of truth. It guarantees transparency, auditable revision histories, and team-wide governance via standard Git pull-request review workflows without incurring operational database overhead.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When architecture decisions (ADRs), system models, schemas, and design guidelines must be reviewable using standard peer code-review processes (e.g., GitHub PRs, GitLab MRs).
  • When development workflows and automated agents require zero-friction offline reads and writes without managing database connections, migrations, or access credentials.
  • When team structures require transparent branching, merging, and distributed revision control for governance artifacts alongside production application code.
  • When building agentic or automated workflows that parse, generate, and ingest structured metadata as static schema-validated files.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• High-frequency transactional mutations: Systems requiring hundreds or thousands of concurrent transactional writes per minute will encounter severe Git merge conflicts and write serialization bottlenecks.
  • Dynamic ad-hoc querying across millions of records: Complex multi-variable joins, analytical aggregation queries, or low-latency index lookups across enterprise-scale data sets require purpose-built SQL/NoSQL or document databases.
  • Granular field-level access control: Environments that enforce column-level or row-level dynamic security boundaries that cannot be mapped to repository directory or branch permission boundaries.

docs.text:
• Knowledge Hierarchy Store (cas-knowledge/): Authoritative tree partitioning architecture artifacts into distinct scopes: global taxonomies, project-specific models, runtime telemetry, and template baselines.
  • Workspace Bootstrapper & Synchronizer (src/cas_runner/bootstrap.py): Provisions foundational directory topologies (init_workspace) and synchronizes centralized governance blocks into downstream repositories (merge_cas_governance_block).
  • Schema Validation Engine (src/cas_runner/validation/): Executes declarative JSON Schema and Markdown syntax validation across all repository files during local development and automated CI stages.

docs.title: Recommended Choices
docs.text:
• Storage Formats: YAML for structured configuration/metadata (human-readable, dense), JSON Schema for deterministic contracts, and Markdown for human-oriented narrative architecture documentation.
  • Version Control Engine: Git with native branching, diff tools, and commit signing to guarantee immutability and provenance tracking.
  • Validation Tools: Python jsonschema, yamllint, and markdownlint integrated into pre-commit hooks and GitHub Actions pipelines.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered & Set Aside
docs.text:
• Relational / Document Databases (PostgreSQL, MongoDB): Rejected due to unnecessary operational complexity, connection lifecycle management, lack of integrated code-review workflows, and difficulty maintaining branching coherence with application code.
  • Enterprise Wiki Solutions (Confluence, Notion): Rejected due to vendor lock-in, proprietary APIs, inability to natively bind schema checks into automated continuous integration pipelines, and friction for automated AI/agentic pipelines.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Monorepo Co-location Variant: Architecture knowledge files live directly inside the primary application repository (docs/architecture/ or cas-knowledge/), ensuring atomic commits when code changes require simultaneous architectural specification updates.
  • Dedicated Centralized Governance Submodule Variant: Architecture artifacts reside in a dedicated corporate governance repository that downstream projects consume as a version-pinned Git submodule or package dependency.
  • Static-Site Generated (SSG) Variant: A headless documentation pipeline (e.g., MkDocs Material, Astro) monitors file system changes and continuously publishes rendered documentation to an internal static portal.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
• Highly resilient against network partitions and service outages; fully functional offline.
  • Immutability and point-in-time recovery are guaranteed natively via Git commit history and SHA hashes.

docs.title: Performance & Latency
docs.text:
• Local disk reads and schema validation complete within milliseconds.
  • Zero network latency for local agentic tooling and development tasks.

docs.title: Cost & Efficiency
docs.text:
• Negligible cost: utilizes existing source control hosting (GitHub, GitLab) with zero database compute or storage licensing fees.
  • Highly efficient storage footprints through text compression and Git blob packing.

docs.title: Operability
docs.text:
• Minimal maintenance surface: standard Git maintenance (e.g., git gc) applies.
  • Universal tool support: editable by any standard text editor, IDE, or CLI utility without bespoke database drivers.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Unchecked Parallel Branch Concurrency: Multiple autonomous agents or team members submitting uncoordinated pull requests modifying the exact same YAML index, generating frequent merge conflicts.
  • Remedy: Partition knowledge into domain-segregated directories or date-partitioned signal files rather than monolithic shared index files.
  • Schema-Free Free-Form Rot: Allowing unconstrained Markdown authoring without automated schema validation, resulting in broken links and drift.
  • Remedy: Enforce strict JSON/YAML schema validation and link checkers in blocking CI gate pipelines.
  • Binary & Media Bloat: Storing large design binaries, screen recordings, or uncompressed exports in the repository.
  • Remedy: Enforce Git LFS or direct external object storage links (e.g., S3) for heavy media assets.

docs.title: Migration Path & Starting Points
docs.text:
1. Initialize a clean directory structure under cas-knowledge/ using src/cas_runner/bootstrap.py.
  2. Define foundational directory contracts (global/, projects/, runtime/, templates/).
  3. Establish pre-commit validation hooks with JSON Schema to enforce metadata consistency prior to repository commits.
  4. Connect continuous integration (CI) linting to validate cross-references and reject non-conforming changes.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Deterministic Governance Action State Machine
Reference Architecture: Deterministic Governance Action State Machine
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Deterministic Governance Action State Machine pattern provides an authoritative boundary that validates, orchestrates, and records lifecycle transitions for governed software, architecture, and deployment artifacts. In environments driven by autonomous multi-agent systems or automated pipelines, non-deterministic agents may attempt invalid state skips, bypass required reviews, or corrupt artifact metadata. This pattern imposes a strict, fail-closed finite state machine (FSM) enforcing transition prerequisites and deterministic state mutations.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When autonomous AI agents or automated pipelines have permissions to mutate artifact lifecycle states (e.g., candidate promotion, architecture deprecation, production certification).
  • In regulated or high-assurance systems where auditability demands verifiable, tamper-evident lineage of who or what initiated each transition.
  • When business or architectural rules mandate strict sequential gates (e.g., code cannot transition to 'promoted' without meeting quality and verification criteria).
  • To centralize scattered transition validation logic into a unified, versioned transition registry.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• In simple CRUD applications where lifecycle progression is linear, single-user, and without multi-step safety invariants.
  • For fluid, exploratory workflows where artifact states are ad-hoc, unstructured, or intentionally non-linear without governance implications.
  • In ultra-low latency data plane processing where state check overhead cannot be tolerated and consistency is eventual.

    Store[("Governance State & Audit Store (Data store)")]

    Agent -->|1. Submit GovernanceAction payload| Engine
    Engine -->|2. Validate transition rules| Registry
    Registry -->|3. Assert valid transition| Engine
    Engine -->|4. Persist mutated state & audit event| Store
