docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• TransitionRegistry (src/cas_runner/governance/governance_action_engine.py): Encapsulates valid lifecycle states and permissible directed transitions between them. Evaluates pre-conditions, required approvals, and invariant assertions before permitting any state mutation.
  • GovernanceActionEngine (src/cas_runner/governance/governance_action_engine.py): Orchestrates governance action requests. Accepts strongly-typed GovernanceAction payloads, queries the TransitionRegistry for validity, executes transactional state modifications, and guarantees fail-closed error handling.
  • Governance Action & Domain Models (src/cas_runner/governance/models.py): Provides immutable schemas for GovernanceAction, State transitions, and the typed GovernanceException hierarchy representing transition violations.
  • Governance State & Audit Store (src/cas_runner/governance/storage.py): Persists current artifact lifecycle states along with immutable, append-only logs capturing actor identities, timestamps, input parameters, and transition rationales.

docs.title: Recommended Technologies
docs.text:
• In-Memory Deterministic FSM Registry (Python / Pydantic / TypedDicts): Enforces compile-time and runtime validation with minimal overhead, natively supporting type validation in src/cas_runner/governance/models.py.
  • Transactional Persistence (PostgreSQL or ACID-compliant Document Store): Guarantees linearizable transition commit and concurrent lock handling to prevent race conditions during parallel state changes.
  • Append-Only Audit Journal (Structured JSON Logs or Event Store): Emits structured telemetry for every transition attempt (both approved and rejected) for compliance auditing.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered & Set Aside
docs.text:
• Decentralized Boolean Flags on Entities: Rejected due to state drift, lack of centralized gatekeeping, and vulnerability to agents directly mutating individual attributes without checking preconditions.
  • Heavyweight External BPMN / Workflow Engines (e.g., Camunda, Temporal): Set aside for local governance operations to avoid external network hops and excessive operational footprint, though appropriate as an outer-loop orchestrator.

docs.title: 1. Synchronous Guarded Execution (Default)
docs.text: The calling process invokes the GovernanceActionEngine synchronously. The engine checks the TransitionRegistry, writes to storage, and returns an updated state or raises a GovernanceException. Ideal for CLI tools and deterministic pipeline steps.

docs.title: 2. Asynchronous Event-Driven FSM
docs.text: State transition intents are published to an event bus. The governance engine acts as an event consumer, validating transitions, writing to an outbox, and broadcasting transition completed/failed events.

docs.title: 3. Dry-Run / Policy Simulation Mode
docs.text: The engine evaluates whether a hypothetical state transition would succeed under current registry rules without persisting mutations, enabling autonomous agents to plan multi-step actions safely.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
• Fail-Closed Guarantees: Any unmapped transition or unmet condition raises a deterministic GovernanceException, preventing unverified state advancement.
  • Concurrency Control: Optimistic locking via version fields or explicit row-level locks ensures parallel agent actions do not cause race conditions.

docs.title: Performance & Latency
docs.text: • O(1) In-Memory Lookup: State validation operates as a constant-time table lookup within TransitionRegistry, keeping overhead below 2 milliseconds.

docs.title: Cost & Efficiency
docs.text: • Low Compute Overhead: Eliminates complex distributed rollbacks and remediation compute costs by preventing invalid operations upfront.

docs.title: Operability & Observability
docs.text:
• Structured Diagnostic Codes: Distinct error codes and structured transition metadata enable real-time alerting on agent hallucination rates or broken pipeline attempts.
  • Complete Audit Trail: Every executed or rejected transition records actor provenance, timestamp, and target state.

docs.title: 1. The 'Bypass Force Flag'
docs.text:
• Anti-pattern: Adding parameters like force=True or skip_validation=True to the action engine to expedite emergency releases.
  • Remedy: Model emergency states as formal transitions in the registry requiring designated break-glass credentials and explicit post-incident audits.

docs.title: 2. Direct State Mutation (Backdoor Updates)
docs.text:
• Anti-pattern: Allowing repository or data access layers to update status fields directly in the database without passing through GovernanceActionEngine.
  • Remedy: Restrict write access to artifact state tables exclusively to the engine service account or encapsulate updates behind an authoritative repository interface.

docs.title: 3. Static Matrix Rot
docs.text:
• Anti-pattern: Hardcoding states without versioning the transition matrix, leading to deadlocks when emerging operational states are introduced.
  • Remedy: Maintain the transition matrix as declarative versioned configuration, validated by automated FSM reachability test suites.

docs.title: Starting Points & Migration Path
docs.text:
1. State Discovery: Map all existing implicit artifact lifecycle states and assemble them into a formal directed state diagram.
  2. Codify Transition Matrix: Instantiate the TransitionRegistry mapping current states to permissible next states, attaching precondition callables.
  3. Intercept Mutation Paths: Refactor all agent action handlers to route through GovernanceActionEngine.execute_transition(action).
  4. Enable Audit Assertion: Introduce integration tests simulating both valid journeys and illegal transition attempts (e.g., skipping review steps) to verify fail-closed behavior.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Grounded Prompt Fact Projection
Reference Architecture: Grounded Prompt Fact Projection
Overview and Purpose
docs.text: The Grounded Prompt Fact Projection pattern deterministically extracts, normalizes, and packages verified repository deltas and architectural registers into strongly typed prompt facts. Its primary goal is to completely eliminate LLM hallucinations during automated governance, architectural review, and decision checks by guaranteeing that reasoning agents operate exclusively over verified capability diffs and historical rules rather than speculative inferences or raw, unparsed git diffs.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• Automated architectural decision agents or governance verification workflows require factual grounds regarding code and metadata changes.
  • Large codebase diffs exceed standard LLM token window limits or introduce high contextual noise that degrades evaluation quality.
  • Auditable, deterministic LLM evaluation pipelines require reproducible prompt contexts with verifiable lineage back to AST nodes or version-controlled deltas.
  • Systems need to decouple the computational overhead of diff parsing and semantic verification from LLM prompt synthesis.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• Open-ended creative generation or exploratory brainstorming where precise structural correctness and architectural invariants are secondary.
  • Single-file trivial diffs or small scripting repositories where raw source text fits within token constraints without prompt noise.
  • Ad-hoc conversational interfaces that lack underlying access to structural ASTs, git revision graphs, or formal architectural state registers.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Delta Extraction Service (src/cas_runner/steering/models.py): Inspects commit ranges, pull requests, and file updates to extract concrete code deltas, AST node transitions, and capability changes.
  • Fact Projection Compiler (src/cas_runner/steering/models.py): Normalizes parsed deltas into typed PromptFact instances, filters irrelevant syntactical churn, and produces the consolidated SteeringRuntimeIndex.
  • Steering Runtime Index Store (.github/workflows/cas-build-steering-projection.yml): Maintains persistent, immutable serialized snapshots of architectural state and projected facts for downstream evaluation workflows.
  • LLM Decision Agent (src/cas_runner/steering/models.py): Ingests serialized prompt facts directly into strict prompt scaffolding to execute deterministic governance assessments without ungrounded hallucinations.

docs.title: Technology Selections
docs.text:
• Data Modeling & Validation: Pydantic / Python Typing (PromptFact, SteeringRuntimeIndex) was chosen to enforce schema guarantees at compile-time and runtime serialization boundaries.
  • Orchestration & Triggering: GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/cas-build-steering-projection.yml) chosen for event-driven generation on pull request and merge commits, ensuring projections stay current with the repository state.
  • Serialization Format: JSON/JSONL with deterministic key ordering, chosen for low-overhead ingestion by standard LLM contexts.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Dynamic Vector Search (RAG): Discarded for governance decision paths because semantic similarity search can retrieve out-of-date or peripherally related snippets while omitting critical breaking signature changes.
  • Raw Git Diff Injection: Discarded due to token context limits, high token consumption costs, and inability of language models to reliably parse large multi-file hunks without hallucinating implicit dependencies.

docs.title: 1. CI-Compiled Batch Projection
docs.text: Projections are compiled as static artifacts during automated pull request or branch build workflows. Downstream agents load pre-computed indices from storage caches, minimizing runtime latency during governance decisions.

docs.title: 2. Ephemeral In-Memory Projection
docs.text: Invoked on-demand in local developer environments or interactive agent loops. Facts are extracted in real-time across working tree dirty buffers without writing persistent artifacts to CI pipelines.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
• Guarantees factual determinism: identical code modifications consistently yield identical PromptFact structures.
  • Eliminates hallucination-driven governance false positives by bounding LLM decision inputs to verified changes.

docs.title: Performance & Latency
docs.text:
• Projection compilation adds modest overhead in CI (< 30 seconds for standard pull requests).
  • Agent evaluation latency decreases significantly because prompt payloads are reduced by 60-80% compared to dumping raw source files or unpruned diffs.

docs.title: Cost & Token Efficiency
docs.text: • Compact fact representation minimizes prompt token usage, yielding major operational cost reductions across high-frequency CI review loops.

docs.title: Operability & Auditability
docs.text: • Every projected fact includes AST symbol anchors and source commit hashes, providing complete forensic traceability from LLM evaluation verdicts back to original source lines.

docs.title: Anti-Pattern 1: Raw Diff Dumping
docs.text:
• Problem: Passing unparsed git diffs straight to the agent prompt.
  • Impact: LLM misses cross-file interface contracts, misinterprets line deletions, and exhausts context windows.
  • Remedy: Force diffs through AST parsing into structured PromptFact models before prompt construction.

docs.title: Anti-Pattern 2: Over-Pruning Semantic Dependencies
docs.text:
• Problem: Slicing diffs too aggressively to save tokens, removing caller/callee context.
  • Impact: Decision agents evaluate changes in isolation and fail to catch cascading architectural breaks.
  • Remedy: Include typed dependency references within the PromptFact schema to capture adjacent interface contracts.

docs.title: Migration Path
docs.text:
1. Model Adoption: Import and configure PromptFact and SteeringRuntimeIndex models from src/cas_runner/steering/models.py.
  2. Pipeline Integration: Deploy .github/workflows/cas-build-steering-projection.yml into target repositories to automate fact compilation on commit triggers.
  3. Agent Binding: Update prompt compilation logic in decision agents to inject the projected index rather than invoking dynamic vector searches or raw file reads.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When engineering teams and autonomous agents produce empirical operational heuristics that need validation before becoming mandatory enterprise standards.
  • In distributed multi-agent systems and platforms where unverified emergent behaviors or local optimizations threaten global system stability if prematurely codified.
  • When formalizing the lifecycle of continuous architecture knowledge from tentative discovery through empirical validation to standard pattern governance.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• For straightforward, one-off configuration changes or tactical software bug fixes that carry no architectural implications.
  • In early-stage rapid prototyping or sandbox experiments where formal promotion overhead slows critical initial product discovery.
  • When adopting well-established, industry-standard protocols (e.g., standard OAuth2, TLS 1.3) where organizational validation cycles are redundant.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Heuristic Ingestion Component (cas-knowledge/templates/heuristic-to-pattern_template.md): Standardizes captured project signals, candidate heuristics, and runtime observations using declarative metadata templates.
  • Promotion Review Engine (cas-knowledge/templates/promotion_decision.md): Verifies that heuristics meet promotion criteria (significance, reusability, evidence quality) and records immutable promotion decisions.
  • Empirical Evidence Store (docs/architecture/cas-pattern-evolution-flow.md): Persists experiment logs, agent steering logs, and multi-project adoption records that justify pattern advancement.
  • Global Pattern Catalogue (docs/architecture/patterns/): Serves as the enterprise source-of-truth repository for promoted patterns ingested by agent planning loops and engineering teams.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
• Git-backed Markdown Schemas: Chosen for transparent diffing, native repository versioning, and auditable pull request reviews.
  • Declarative Template Validation: Markdown and JSON schemas define necessary criteria before transition states trigger.
  • Alternatives Considered: Centralized CMDBs and wiki software were evaluated but rejected due to synchronization lag, lack of branchability, and inability to integrate directly into agent context windows.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Asynchronous Batch Review: Promotion readiness metrics aggregate periodically, producing scheduled promotion batches for human architecture review.
  • Event-Driven Continuous Review: Promotion decisions trigger immediately upon an empirical signal reaching pre-set confidence and reuse thresholds across projects.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: High auditability via immutable Git-backed decision logs, ensuring clear lineage from raw heuristic to promoted pattern.
  • Performance & Latency: Deliberate governance buffer prevents hasty standard adoption; metric ingestion is non-blocking to runtime applications.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Low operational footprint relying on standard version control and lightweight template evaluation rather than proprietary governance infrastructure.
  • Operability: Clear state transitions (heuristic -> candidate -> validated pattern) reduce ambiguity in automated agent reasoning.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Premature Codification: Elevating a localized, idiosyncratic heuristic directly into global architecture patterns without multi-project validation, leading to architectural bloat.
  • Orphaned Heuristic Silo: Allowing valuable heuristics to remain unreviewed due to lack of explicit review tooling or designated ownership.
  • Metric-Only Promotion: Automating pattern promotion without human-in-the-loop review for high-impact architectural constraints.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
• Starting Point: Incorporate heuristic-to-pattern_template.md into local development repositories to record emergent patterns during sprint retrospectives.
  • Migration Path: Gradually expose empirical evidence templates to automated agent workflows for telemetry capture, followed by establishing architecture review gates.
  • Governance Ownership: Platform Architecture Guild (domain_id: continuous-architecture, initiative_id: agentic-governance).

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Architecture Work Registry as Authoritative Backlog
Reference Architecture: Architecture Work Registry as Authoritative Backlog
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Architecture Work Registry pattern decouples authoritative architectural planning, decision records, and intent backlogs from ephemeral derived dashboards or regenerated artifacts. In automated continuous architecture pipelines, discovery extractors and visualization tools frequently synthesize projections such as Architecture Evolution Maps (AEMs). Embedding planning state directly inside generated views creates severe risk of data loss upon regeneration. Establishing a dedicated, machine-readable Architecture Work registry ensures all planned, in-flight, and completed architectural initiatives persist deterministically as the single source of truth.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When automated pipelines periodically regenerate architectural roadmaps, dependency graphs, or evolution maps from code and telemetry.
  • When multiple engineers or automated agents contribute architectural work items and decisions that must persist independently of UI visualizations.
  • When governance audits require verifiable historical lineage of architectural decisions decoupled from ephemeral reporting tools.
  • When reconciling discrepancy between discovered code state and planned target architectures.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• In simple monolithic or small-scale applications where architectural changes are tracked directly within standard issue trackers without automated architecture evolution map synthesis.
  • When architecture visualization is purely descriptive and static with no automated regeneration or bi-directional lifecycle synchronization.
  • When planning state is managed strictly through an external enterprise tool (e.g., Jira Enterprise Portfolio) that already maintains authoritative change webhooks into codebase pipelines.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Architecture Work Registry (catalogue/work_registry.json): Authoritative datastore maintaining structured records of planned, active, and completed architectural initiatives, ensuring intent is preserved across discovery cycles.
  • AEM Generator Step (src/cas_runner/steps/aem_generator.py): Automated workflow step that reads authoritative planning items from the registry alongside codebase telemetry to synthesize evolution mappings.
  • Source Code Telemetry Extractor (src/cas_runner/extractors/): Parses project source code and metadata to derive the current structural state without modifying planning backlogs.
  • Derived Architecture Evolution Map (AEM) (docs/architecture/aem_report.md): Ephemeral or regenerated presentation artifact illustrating historical progression, active delta, and projected target architectures.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
• Authoritative Backlog Format: Machine-readable JSON/YAML files versioned in Git. Alternatives considered: SQL Database (rejected due to git-branch mismatch and review friction), JIRA/Linear API (set aside to avoid runtime dependencies during CI/CD generation runs).
  • Pipeline Runner: Python-based runner executing deterministic steps (src/cas_runner). Alternatives considered: Bash scripts (insufficient typing and validation) and cloud workflows (overly complex for repository-local artifact generation).
  • Serialization Standards: JSON Schema validation on work registry records to enforce semantic validation prior to map generation runs.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Synchronous Commit-Hook Validation: Work items are validated against JSON schema in pre-commit hooks, ensuring invalid schema never enters the authoritative branch.
  • Asynchronous Pipeline Reconciliation: Automated CI/CD actions reconcile work items against actual codebase structural changes, flagging completed or drifting initiatives.
  • Strict Decoupled Visualization Mode: Derived views (AEM) are strictly read-only and overwritten on every merge, preventing manual edits from leaking into presentation views.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Eliminates data loss during map regeneration by isolating mutable planning state from generated presentation outputs.
  • Performance & Latency: Local file-based ingestion and synthesis yields sub-second map generation during continuous integration runs.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Relies on repository storage and local processing, incurring zero auxiliary database or SaaS subscription licensing overhead.
  • Operability: Straightforward Git revision history provides immutable change logs and trivial rollback capabilities for architectural decisions.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Direct View Editing: Modifying derived Architecture Evolution Map markdown or diagrams directly instead of updating the Architecture Work Registry, causing manual changes to be overwritten on next discovery run (Remedy: Treat derived files as build artifacts with clear generated warnings).
  • Monolithic State Blobbing: Storing both codebase AST scans and human planning rationales inside the same mutable JSON file (Remedy: Enforce explicit separation between authoritative registry and extracted telemetry).
  • Silent Intent Drift: Marking architectural work complete in the registry without corresponding verifiable structural code changes (Remedy: Implement automated reconciliation checks during CI).

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text: Begin adoption by extracting existing architectural notes and backlog items into a dedicated directory or structured JSON file (work_registry.json). Configure generation tools (such as aem_generator.py) to treat this file as read-only input. Establish governance ownership under the platform architecture team (governance_domain: core-platform, initiative_id: cas-governance-registry). Ensure pull request templates require registry entries for any systemic structural changes.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Authoritative Backlog Separation Pattern
Reference Architecture: Authoritative Backlog Separation Pattern
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: This pattern establishes a strict separation between authoritative, write-mastered architecture change backlog items and regenerated, read-only downstream views or projection dashboards.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When managing architecture roadmaps, technical debt, and change initiatives across distributed teams where derived reporting dashboards are frequently regenerated from underlying repositories or state stores.
  • When multiple stakeholders need bespoke reporting formats (Kanban boards, executive summaries, compliance matrix views) without introducing split-brain mutations to the core backlog.
  • When automated CI/CD pipelines synthesize architecture state and projection views from structured YAML/JSON metadata or version-controlled records.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• In simple, single-team projects where a single issue tracker (e.g., Jira or GitHub Issues) serves natively as both the authoritative write store and the presentation interface.
  • When real-time, bi-directional collaborative spreadsheet editing is an explicit operational requirement with no authoritative schema enforcement.
  • For short-lived spike initiatives where the operational overhead of projection pipelines outweighs the risk of data divergence.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Backlog Ingestion Service (services/backlog-ingestion): Validates schema adherence, enforces immutability and provenance tracking, and persists change items into the authoritative store.
  • Authoritative Backlog Store (storage/backlog-master): Single source of truth repository for all backlog items, maintaining cryptographic audit histories and structured state transitions.
  • Projection Engine (workers/projection-pipeline): Executes declarative projection rules to transform authoritative backlog items into downstream presentation schemas and report artifacts.
  • Read-Only Dashboards & Views (frontend/architecture-views): Provides stakeholders with read-only visualization, filtering, and export capabilities without accepting write transactions.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text: Recommended choices include Git-backed structured storage (YAML/JSON schemas under Git LFS or repository trees) for transparent version control and branch-based approvals, paired with static site generation (Astro, MkDocs, or Next.js static exports) for projection rendering. Automated transformations run via GitHub Actions or event-driven workers. Alternatives considered and set aside: Bi-directional synchronization tools (e.g., syncing Notion/Jira directly with two-way webhooks) were rejected due to merge conflict anomalies, loss of schema integrity, and race conditions leading to overwritten authoritative edits.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Event-Driven Projections: Changes to the authoritative store emit change events via a message bus (Kafka/EventBridge), triggering instant projection pipeline updates.
  • Scheduled Static Regeneration: Batch projection generation executed on a periodic cron or CI trigger, optimizing for cost and static hosting predictability.
  • Ephemeral Query-Time Projection: Projections are computed on-the-fly via serverless API lambdas caching read-optimized snapshots in Redis.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: High resilience through decoupled read/write planes; failure in projection workers does not affect authoritative data durability.
  • Performance & Latency: Instantaneous read speeds via pre-rendered static artifacts or materialized caches; ingestion validation latencies under 200ms.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Low operational cost using static hosting (S3/CloudFront) and on-demand compute for transformation workflows.
  • Operability: Zero-downtime schema evolution enabled by regenerating projection snapshots from the immutable authoritative baseline.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Direct-Edit Trap: Allowing end users to edit derived projection views (e.g., spreadsheets or Kanban boards) directly, causing edits to be wiped during the next projection run. Remedy: Enforce read-only access on projections and route all edits through the authoritative ingestion path.
  • Dual-Source Mutation: Accepting changes in both the master store and external sync targets with heuristic reconcilers. Remedy: Designate the backlog store as strictly unidirectional.
  • Unversioned Authoritative Schemas: Storing backlog entries without explicit semantic versioning, breaking projection parser pipelines. Remedy: Enforce strict JSON Schema validation during ingestion.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text: Start by identifying the current canonical repository for backlog items and marking all secondary reporting tools as read-only. Implement automated projection builds in CI to replace manual dashboard curation. Governance ownership: Managed by the Architecture Governance Working Group under Domain: governance-core, Initiative: architecture-enablement. Inquiries should be routed to the Lead Enterprise Architect.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Continuous Architecture Governance Runtime
Reference Architecture: Continuous Architecture Governance Runtime
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Continuous Architecture Governance Runtime operationalises continuous architecture steering by implementing an automated closed-loop lifecycle (Detect -> Analyse -> Plan -> Execute -> Publish -> Observe) within CI/CD delivery pipelines. It prevents and remediates architectural drift without manual intervention for non-breaking changes, replacing slow, manual review boards with deterministic policy evaluation.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When architectural drift between design models and deployed codebases causes recurring delivery blockers or production incidents.
  • In high-velocity multi-repo or monorepo environments where manual Architecture Review Boards (ARBs) create a throughput bottleneck (e.g., 15:1 developer-to-architect ratio).
  • When architectural decisions (ADRs) can be codified into computable fitness functions, schema assertions, or static policy rules.
  • In engineering organisations targeting continuous compliance, regulatory traceability, or autonomous refactoring for non-breaking architectural updates.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• In early-stage exploratory prototypes or disposable greenfield proof-of-concepts where architecture undergoes radical daily pivots and schemas are intentionally unstable.
  • In teams lacking automated CI/CD pipelines, automated testing, or source-controlled architecture definitions.
  • For subjective or high-ambiguity domain modelling decisions that inherently require cross-functional consensus and stakeholder negotiation rather than rule-based automated verification.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Drift Detector Agent (src/governance/drift-detector): Inspects commit deltas, AST structures, infrastructure-as-code manifests, and service dependency graphs to detect divergence against recorded architecture state.
  • Fitness Policy Engine (src/governance/policy-engine): Executes declarative architecture fitness functions and compliance rules against detected drift to evaluate impact severity and identify policy violations.
  • Plan & Execution Controller (src/governance/execution-controller): Orchestrates automated remediation workflows, synthesizes Architecture Work Items, and generates safe automated pull requests or blocking signals.
  • Architecture State Store (docs/architecture/state): Maintains authoritative machine-readable current architecture state snapshots, architecture decision records (ADRs), and pattern catalogues.

docs.title: Recommended Technologies
docs.text:
• Policy Enforcement Engine: Open Policy Agent (OPA) / Rego or TypeScript-based structural linters (e.g., ArchUnit for JVM, ts-arch for TypeScript). Rationale: Declarative policy as code enables version-controlled, auditable governance assertions inside standard CI runners.
  • State Storage: Git-backed Markdown/JSON Schema repository (Architecture-as-Code). Rationale: Eliminates synchronization drift between documentation and code; benefits from Git history, PR reviews, and cryptographic commit signing.
  • Orchestration: GitHub Actions / GitLab CI custom actions running in containerized runtimes. Rationale: Integrates natively into developer pull request workflows without requiring external orchestration servers.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered & Set Aside
docs.text:
• Centralized CMDB / Governance Web Portal: Rejected due to high operational latency, disjointed developer experience, stale manual synchronization, and inability to gate pull requests directly.
  • Fully Autonomous LLM Fixer without Deterministic Gates: Rejected due to nondeterministic hallucination risks on structural dependencies and lack of formal safety guarantees.

docs.title: Variant A: Observability & Soft Governance (Advisory Mode)
docs.text: Operates asynchronously on merged branches or daily schedules. Evaluates policies and publishes warnings, architecture health scores, and Jira/Linear work items without blocking CI pipelines. Recommended for initial onboarding and legacy systems.

docs.title: Variant B: Deterministic Pull-Request Gate (Enforcing Mode)
docs.text: Runs synchronously inside pull-request checks. Fails build checks if critical architectural invariants (e.g., cyclic boundary violations, unauthorized data access layers) are broken, while auto-committing non-breaking remediations (e.g., manifest schema alignment).

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
• Idempotent execution: Multiple runs on the same commit hash produce identical evaluation states.
  • Graceful degradation: CI builds can be configured with safe fallback modes during governance engine transient failures to avoid blocking critical hotfixes.

docs.title: Performance & Latency
docs.text:
• Pipeline Execution Overhead: Must complete evaluation within <= 45 seconds for incremental PR checks to preserve developer feedback velocity.
  • Caching: Employs distributed AST and dependency graph caching between runs to prevent repeated full-repository scanning.

docs.title: Cost & Efficiency
docs.text: • Serverless / Ephemeral Execution: Runs within existing CI runner allocations without requiring permanent dedicated infrastructure instances.

docs.title: Operability & Auditability
docs.text: • Cryptographic Audit Trail: Every architectural evaluation, pass/fail result, and drift remediation is recorded directly in Git history and pipeline logs, meeting enterprise compliance standards.

docs.title: Anti-Pattern 1: The 'All-Blocking Day One' Gate
docs.text:
• Pitfall: Imposing strict blocking enforcement across dozens of newly codified rules on day one, stalling all team deliveries and causing developers to bypass checks.
  • Remedy: Start in Variant A (Advisory Mode) to build baseline drift metrics, tuning false positives before enabling synchronous gating for high-severity invariants only.

docs.title: Anti-Pattern 2: Unversioned External Governance Authority
docs.text:
• Pitfall: Pointing CI runners to a dynamically updated remote policy endpoint without pinned semantic versions, causing unexpected build failures on untouched legacy repositories.
  • Remedy: Pin architecture governance engines and rule definitions to immutable semantic versions in the repository manifest.

docs.title: Anti-Pattern 3: Opaque Rule Failures
docs.text:
• Pitfall: Failing a developer's build with generic errors such as 'Architecture policy violated' without contextual guidance.
  • Remedy: Provide actionable error annotations pointing directly to the violated ADR, the line of code, and a deterministic remediation guide.

docs.title: Starting Points & Migration Path
docs.text:
1. Phase 1 (Baseline Capture): Extract current architecture boundaries and declare them in machine-readable format (architecture-state.json).
  2. Phase 2 (Advisory CI Integration): Deploy the Drift Detector Agent into CI in reporting-only mode to measure baseline drift frequency and calibrate rules.
  3. Phase 3 (Selective Enforcement): Transition critical perimeter rules (e.g., public API contracts, modular boundary leaks) to blocking gates.
  4. Phase 4 (Autonomous Closed-Loop): Enable automated PR generation for routine updates (e.g., schema refactors, catalog updates).

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Continuous Architecture Governance Loop
Reference Architecture: Continuous Architecture Governance Loop
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Continuous Architecture Governance Loop operationalizes architectural decision enforcement by embedding automated detection, static verification, and drift analysis directly into CI/CD pipelines. It shifts architecture reviews left, transforming intermittent governance gates into continuous automated feedback loops.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• Microservice or modular enterprise codebases where distributed teams introduce silent architectural drift, boundary violations, or unauthorized pattern deviations.
  • Environments experiencing governance review bottlenecks (e.g., 15:1 developer-to-architect ratios) where manual design reviews delay release cycles.
  • Projects requiring verifiable compliance with architectural decisions, structural contracts, and published enterprise standards at pull-request evaluation time.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• Early-stage, exploratory prototypes or throwaway spikes where architectural contracts change daily and enforcement overhead slows innovation.
  • Monolithic codebases with small, co-located teams where direct verbal alignment and simple static linters sufficiently manage system boundaries.
  • Teams without mature automated CI/CD pipelines or baseline version control automation.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Pipeline Trigger (.github/workflows/cas-continuous-architecture.yml): Listens for repository events (pull requests, merges) and initiates automated architectural validation jobs.
  • Drift Detector (src/cas_runner/governance/drift_detector.py): Computes semantic and structural differences between changed code and documented architectural contracts.
  • Governance Validator (src/cas_runner/governance/governance_validator.py): Evaluates architectural rules, module boundaries, schema invariants, and compliance against machine-readable ADRs.
  • Architecture Decision Store (docs/architecture/): Persists machine-readable architecture decisions (ADRs), schemas, and pattern definitions in version-controlled storage.
  • Developer Feedback Adapter (src/cas_runner/governance/reporters/): Emits PR status checks, inline review annotations, and dashboard metrics summarizing governance conformance.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
Recommended Technology Choices: - Pipeline Orchestration: GitHub Actions or GitLab CI runners utilizing containerized execution steps for repeatable static evaluation. - Policy Engine: Python-based structural validation (custom AST and dependency graph analyzers) combined with JSON Schema / Open Policy Agent (OPA) for declarative governance policies. - Data Formats: Markdown-based Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) with embedded YAML/JSON frontmatter to maintain human and machine readability simultaneously.

Alternatives Considered and Set Aside: - Standalone SonarQube Rules: Rejected as primary architecture gate due to limited semantic understanding of domain-specific architectural boundaries and ADR references. - Synchronous Architect Review Gates: Rejected due to velocity drag and linear scaling bottlenecks across scaling product squads.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Advisory / Warning Variant: Executes checks on pull requests and surfaces findings as non-blocking comments or annotations; ideal during initial enterprise rollouts.
  • Enforcing / Blocking Variant: Hard gates PR merging when critical architectural invariants, cross-boundary dependencies, or missing ADR references are detected.
  • Automated Remediation Variant: Detects drift and automatically proposes fix-up PRs or updates architectural indices for non-functional documentation drift.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Pipeline steps run idempotently against fixed commit SHAs; results are deterministic without network flakes.
  • Performance & Latency: Validation executes within 45-90 seconds by performing incremental dependency tree analysis rather than full compilation.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Minimal compute overhead utilizing existing CI/CD runners without specialized hardware requirements.
  • Operability: Governance logs are surfaced directly into developer PR consoles with actionable remediation steps.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Self-Triggering CI Loops: Automated documentation updates or bot commits re-triggering the governance loop infinitely. Remedy: Add explicit [skip ci] directives or bot author suppression.
  • Binary All-or-Nothing Enforcement: Turning on blocking enforcement across a legacy codebase instantly. Remedy: Enforce rules exclusively on changed files, backporting standards gradually via ratcheting thresholds.
  • Disconnected Governance Policies: Enforcing rules that have no corresponding approved ADR or human explanation. Remedy: Require every governance validator check to link to a canonical ADR identifier.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
1. Audit Phase: Deploy .github/workflows/cas-continuous-architecture.yml in warning-only mode to measure baseline drift and rule violation frequency.
  2. Calibration Phase: Refine rule boundaries and suppress known technical debt via explicit exclusion configurations.
  3. Hard-Gate Enforcement: Transition critical boundary rules to required status checks on primary branch pull requests.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Forensic AST Boundary Isolation
Reference Architecture: Forensic AST Boundary Isolation
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: Forensic AST Boundary Isolation establishes strict architectural and execution decoupling between target codebase source files and the static analysis governance runner frameworks that evaluate them. When inspecting code for conformance, dependencies, or architectural compliance, governance tools frequently ingest abstract syntax trees (ASTs) or perform reflection. Without formal boundary isolation, runner libraries, harness dependencies, and governance runtime frameworks bleed into target AST symbols, yielding false positive policy breaches or contaminated dependency graphs.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• Automated architecture governance pipelines that parse target repository codebases to extract static dependency topologies, module boundaries, or import graphs.
  • Polyglot or multi-version codebases where the analysis engine runs in a specific runtime (e.g., Node.js or Python) but must accurately evaluate external target source trees without confusing runtime environment packages with repository dependencies.
  • High-compliance forensic audits where target repository symbols and call sites must maintain cryptographic or verifiable provenance free from test runner or runner harness artifacts.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• Lightweight linters (e.g., standard ESLint, Flake8) executing within native runtime processes where runner isolation overhead exceeds static linting requirements.
  • Dynamic runtime profiling or agent-based instrumentation where the target application must purposefully link against telemetry or APM harnesses at runtime.
  • Monolithic codebases evaluated solely through compiler-native toolchains without custom governance extractors.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    runner["Runner Orchestrator (Container)"]
    sandbox["Isolated AST Sandbox (Container)"]
    extractor["Empirical Discovery Engine (Container)"]
    repoStore[("Target Repository FS (Data store)")]
    evidenceStore[("Forensic Graph Evidence Store (Data store)")]
    governanceEngine["Governance Rules Engine (External System)"]

    runner -->|1. Mount target codebase| repoStore
    runner -->|2. Instantiate ephemeral context| sandbox
    sandbox -->|3. Read untainted source| repoStore
    sandbox -->|4. Parse AST in clean scope| extractor
    extractor -->|5. Write verified evidence| evidenceStore
    governanceEngine -->|6. Query isolated facts| evidenceStore

    classDef container fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef store fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef external fill:#666666,stroke:#333333,color:#fff
    class runner,sandbox,extractor container
    class repoStore,evidenceStore store
    class governanceEngine external

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Runner Orchestrator (governance/runner/orchestrator): Initiates the analysis session, enforces container- or process-level isolation boundaries, and provides clean mounting of the target codebase without injecting governance dependencies into the target path.
  • Isolated AST Sandbox (governance/sandbox/ast_boundary): Executes out-of-process language parsers within an unprivileged execution context, filtering host environment variables, module resolution search paths, and synthetic wrappers.
  • Empirical Discovery Engine (governance/discovery/extractor): Extracts structural symbols, module imports, and architectural boundary markers, ensuring all detected nodes originate solely within target repository boundaries.
  • Target Repository FS (/mnt/target_repo): Read-only filesystem mount containing raw target repository source files, configuration manifests, and project-level lockfiles.
  • Forensic Graph Evidence Store (governance/storage/evidence): Immutable persistence store holding verified AST extraction evidence schemas and verified relationship records.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
Selected Technology Stack: - Language-Agnostic Tree-Sitter Bindings: Chosen for AST parsing over language-native eval/reflection mechanisms (e.g., Python ast module or Babel parser run directly in runner context). Tree-sitter produces concrete syntax trees without invoking the language's native runtime loader, eliminating ambient path resolution bugs. - Ephemeral Process Sandboxing (Rootless Linux Containers / namespaces): Isolates file resolution and ensures runner libraries cannot be traversed during AST node graph building.

Alternatives Considered and Set Aside: - Native Dynamic Module Loader / Reflection: Rejected due to frequent symbol contamination, namespace collisions with runner utility packages, and security risks associated with loading untrusted target code. - Universal Regex / Heuristic Scanning: Set aside due to high false-positive rates with complex syntax, multi-line declarations, and scoped namespace aliases.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Strict Out-of-Process Sandbox: Executes Tree-sitter parsers inside isolated child processes with dedicated memory spaces and restricted filesystem views. Ideal for CI/CD runners analyzing untrusted code or complex monorepos.
  • Language Daemon IPC Boundary: Employs dedicated long-running language server daemons (LSP) across local Unix domain sockets to parse target ASTs, maximizing throughput when scanning high-churn multi-project repositories while preserving strict memory isolation.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Eliminates governance pipeline flakiness and false-positive policy rejections triggered by runner harness dependencies leaking into discovery scans.
  • Performance & Latency: Introduces minimal overhead (~5-15% increase compared to in-process parsing) due to IPC boundary context switches, mitigated by streaming AST chunks.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Low memory footprint; unprivileged sandbox worker pools scale down to zero when analysis phases complete.
  • Operability: Yields clean, reproducible evidence trees with source mapping hash checks, simplifying forensic debugging and audit tracking.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Ambient Classpath / Node Module Leaking: Allowing the runner harness's node_modules or PYTHONPATH to overlay the target repository's search path, causing the AST extractor to identify governance packages as target dependencies. Remedy: Mount target code in a scrubbed execution environment with blank module search paths.
  • In-Process Reflection: Invoking require() or importlib.import_module() on target components inside the governance runner context to introspect structure. Remedy: Parse syntax trees statically without evaluating runtime imports.
  • Single-Pass Monolithic Parser: Reusing a single parser state across disparate subprojects without purging scope caches between microservice modules in a monorepo. Remedy: Instantiate fresh sandbox worker contexts per bounded context or workspace.

docs.title: Starting Points & Migration Path
docs.text:
1. Phase 1 (Audit): Audit existing architectural governance extractors to catalog runner dependencies present in scanner lockfiles.
  2. Phase 2 (Decoupling): Refactor AST parsing calls to run via isolated CLI workers or out-of-process Tree-sitter bindings, passing file paths via explicit read-only mounts.
  3. Phase 3 (Verification): Introduce verification assertion assertions in CI to reject any extracted AST evidence containing runner-scoped packages.

docs.title: Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Proposal-Only Steering Projection pattern decouples automated architecture evaluation and projection synthesis from target file mutation. Instead of writing directly to operational governance branches or authoritative steering documents during continuous integration runs, the system emits immutable projection artifacts in a dry-run or proposal mode. Synchronization into authoritative steering files is strictly mediated through downstream, automated pull requests or staging branches, preserving human oversight and preventing race conditions.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• Automated architecture evaluation workflows generate authoritative steering models or status matrices that must be version-controlled.
  • Multiple asynchronous triggers (e.g., commit pushes, scheduled drift checks, governance audits) evaluate architecture states concurrently, risking file write conflicts on the trunk branch.
  • Architecture changes and governance drift require human verification and formal review prior to becoming authoritative operational baselines.
  • Continuous delivery pipelines require non-destructive verification runs without state pollution in operational repos.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• The generated artifacts are purely ephemeral runtime state caches that do not define authoritative policy or architecture truth.
  • Real-time synchronous steering enforcement where immediate inline mutation is required to unblock a deployment pipeline.
  • Low-complexity personal projects where human-in-the-loop review overhead outweighs the risk of trunk corruption.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Projection Generation Engine (.github/workflows/cas-build-steering-projection.yml): Executes evaluation suites against repo state in proposal-only mode, generating immutable JSON/Markdown projection bundles without pushing directly to protected branches.
  • Projection Artifact Store (actions/upload-artifact): Temporarily persists structured projection bundles, diff reports, and generation metadata across pipeline boundaries.
  • Managed Steering Synchronizer (.github/workflows/cas-managed-steering-sync.yml): Consumes verified projection bundles, performs selective section reconciliation against target files, and submits atomic pull requests against trunk.
  • Authoritative Architecture State (docs/architecture/steering/): Stores the version-controlled, human-reviewed, and authoritative enterprise steering models.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
Recommended Technology Choices: - GitHub Actions Workflow Orchestration: Standardized CI/CD runners providing isolated build environments and native secret handling. - Ephemeral Pipeline Artifacts: Native build artifacts (e.g., actions/upload-artifact) ensure tamper-resistant intermediate transfers without provisioning persistent external object storage. - GitHub PR Integration (gh CLI / create-pull-request action): Standard automated PR creation enabling native git review workflows, branch protection integration, and automated CI check enforcement. - AST/Markdown Diff Patching: Specialized JSON/Markdown diffing engines to isolate changes strictly to managed sections without obliterating manual annotations.

Alternatives Considered & Set Aside: - Direct Commit via Service Account: Rejected due to trunk mutation race conditions, bypass of branch protection rules, and lack of human review auditability. - External SaaS Orchestrator: Considered for central governance tracking, but rejected to maintain zero-dependency in-repo GitOps governance.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Single-Branch Proposal Mode: The pipeline generates an isolated branch named projection/<timestamp> and submits a PR directly for each delta.
  • Idempotent Sync Branch (Rebasing): The synchronizer updates a persistent branch (steering/candidate-sync). If a PR is already open, it updates the existing PR rather than creating duplicates.
  • Shadow Audit Variant: Projection runs purely evaluate and output diffs to CI run summaries and issue comments without creating PRs, suitable for read-only audit environments.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Eliminates race conditions on trunk branch pushes from parallel CI triggers. Failures during projection generation leave authoritative files completely untouched.
  • Performance & Latency: Decouples heavy projection calculations from trunk branch updates. Generation overhead is strictly bounded within isolated pipeline runners with intermediate artifact caching.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Avoids persistent compute overhead by leveraging serverless CI runner minutes only when triggers fire. Prevents pipeline thrashing and merge queue bottlenecks on trunk.
  • Operability: Clear audit trails: All modifications are represented as discrete pull requests with automated diff summaries. Rollbacks follow standard git workflow.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Auto-Merging Unreviewed Proposal PRs: Automatically approving and merging PRs without sanity checks negates the safety guarantees of proposal isolation. Remedy: Enforce required code reviews or strict automated policy validation checks prior to merge.
  • Review Fatigue & PR Flooding: Generating a new PR on every micro-commit creates noise and unmerged PR accumulation. Remedy: Implement branch reuse/rebasing logic in the synchronizer workflow to update existing open projection PRs.
  • Whole-File Overwrites: Replacing entire governance files rather than managed blocks, erasing human edits. Remedy: Use targeted block delimiters (e.g., <!-- BEGIN MANAGED STEERING -->) during synchronization reconciliation.

docs.title: Starting Points
docs.text:
1. Configure your generation workflow (cas-build-steering-projection.yml) to emit outputs into an ephemeral artifact directory rather than executing git push.
  2. Implement a companion sync workflow (cas-managed-steering-sync.yml) triggered upon artifact publication or schedule to reconcile managed anchors.
  3. Establish repository branch protection rules mandating review for any PR touching authoritative governance paths.

docs.title: Migration Path
docs.text:
• Phase 1: Run projection workflow in shadow mode (upload artifacts only, logging diffs).
  • Phase 2: Enable PR generation to an experimental branch without auto-merging.
  • Phase 3: Enforce branch protection on architecture paths and route all automated updates via proposal PRs.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Pattern Scope Classification Framework
Reference Architecture: Pattern Scope Classification Framework
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Pattern Scope Classification Framework establishes a formalized taxonomy and automated evaluation pipeline for segmenting emerging architectural knowledge into explicit governance scopes: Global, Domain, Project, and Local. It ensures architectural patterns are governed at the appropriate organizational tier without premature global standardization.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When decentralized teams discover or build reusable architectural patterns that warrant evaluation for broader enterprise or domain adoption.
  • When cross-project architecture synthesis pipelines need automated heuristics to categorize candidate patterns.
  • When governing large software ecosystems requiring clear boundaries between localized implementation details and enterprise-wide architectural mandates.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• When working within isolated, single-team codebases where all decisions are inherently local and cross-boundary reuse is absent.
  • When evaluating micro-optimizations, internal component refactorings, or language-specific syntax conventions.
  • When centralized command-and-control governance already predefines every architectural construct with no bottom-up pattern discovery.

docs.text:

    classifier -->|2. Score reusability and scope| classifier
    classifier -->|3. Persist scoped metadata| catalogue
    classifier -->|4. Trigger promotion gate| govBoard

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Candidate Ingestion Pipeline (src/cas_runner/steps/candidate_detector.py): Detects and ingests candidate pattern signals from source code repositories, ADR collections, and architectural work streams.
  • Pattern Scope Classifier (src/cas_runner/steps/pattern_scope_classifier.py): Applies deterministic evaluation criteria across scope dimensions (Global, Domain, Project, Local), calculating promotion readiness, significance, and evidence strength.
  • Pattern Catalogue Store (knowledge/projects/ideas-to-life-cas/reference-architectures/): Provides persistent storage for synthesized reference architectures, scope metadata, and associated governance rationales.
  • Governance Review Gateway (src/cas_runner/governance/promotion_gateway.py): Manages the interface between automated classification decisions and human architectural governance bodies for formal sign-off.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+ & Pydantic V2: Selected for deterministic parsing, data validation, and strict schema compliance across pattern artifacts.
  • Git-Backed Markdown & Plain Mermaid: Standardizes documentation formats directly in source repositories, enabling review via pull requests without proprietary tooling.
  • Alternatives Set Aside: Traditional centralized wiki portals were rejected due to configuration drift and lack of programmatic CI/CD integration.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Continuous Pipeline Mode: Runs automatically on every pull request or architectural commit to classify patterns in real time.
  • Batch Governance Mode: Gathers candidate patterns across quarterly or sprint boundaries for collective enterprise review.
  • Conservative Local-Default Mode: Automatically places disputed or ambiguous patterns into project or local scope pending explicit cross-domain validation.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Deterministic classification logic guarantees repeatable scope categorization for identical input evidence.
  • Performance & Latency: Lightweight heuristic evaluation executes in sub-second latency within CI workflows.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Serverless, zero-infrastructure footprint relying on existing Git pipelines and local compute.
  • Operability: Emits machine-readable validation outputs along with contextual markdown rationales to streamline review workflows.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Scope Creep / Premature Global Codification: Elevating an unproven pattern directly to global enterprise status, inflicting premature constraints on unrelated domains. Remedy: Mandate multi-domain evidence verification before global promotion.
  • Classification Deadlock: Stalling pattern adoption when patterns exhibit overlapping domain and project traits. Remedy: Default to the lower scope tier with automated re-evaluation triggers.
  • Unmaintained Catalogues: Accumulating dead records without lifecycle checks. Remedy: Implement deprecation and retirement signals in the classification pipeline.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
1. Integrate pattern_scope_classifier.py into the target project's build and architecture synthesis pipeline.
  2. Configure promotion threshold parameters and register domain architectural review leads.
  3. Establish baseline pattern storage paths under knowledge/projects/<project-name>/reference-architectures/.
  4. Route proposed scope changes through standard repository review processes.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Provider-Agnostic LLM Gateway with Dual Client Contract
Reference Architecture: Provider-Agnostic LLM Gateway with Dual Client Contract
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: Abstracts language model calls behind a standardized client interface, providing production-grade multi-provider connectivity alongside deterministic mock implementations. This ensures agent orchestration components remain completely decoupled from provider SDK evolutions and external network state.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When building autonomous agent workflows, pipelines, or reasoning engines that consume foundation model completions and embeddings across multiple target providers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure OpenAI).
  • When continuous integration pipelines and automated unit testing suites require hermetic, offline execution without incurring live token consumption costs or leaking live credentials.
  • When enterprise governance mandates runtime model interchangeability, automated fallback routing, or dynamic token rate-limiting without refactoring business logic.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• Simple, one-off proof-of-concept scripts or command-line prototypes where coupling to a single vendor SDK incurs minimal technical debt.
  • Scenarios demanding deep, proprietary hardware-specific or provider-exclusive features that cannot be generalized behind a standard completion contract without extensive leaky abstractions.
  • Ultra-low latency micro-benchmarks or embedded edge inferencing where protocol translation overhead cannot be tolerated.

docs.text:

    gateway["LLM Gateway Interface (Container)"]

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• LLM Gateway Interface (src/cas_runner/llm/client_interface.py): The core contract establishing completion, streaming, and tool execution signatures.
  • LiteLLM Client Adapter (src/cas_runner/llm/litellm_client.py): Runtime production gateway translating standardized domain requests into multi-vendor upstream calls.
  • Mock LLM Client (src/cas_runner/llm/mock_client.py): Offline test double that validates request shapes and returns predefined fixtures.
  • Agent Orchestrator (src/cas_runner/orchestrator/agent.py): Consuming domain service implementing business logic purely against the abstract client interface.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
• Recommended Standard: Python Abstract Base Classes with Pydantic v2 schemas for strongly typed request/response boundaries. Use litellm as the translation engine to benefit from built-in retry backoff and vendor parameter normalization.
  • Alternatives Set Aside:
  • Direct vendor SDKs (e.g., openai, anthropic): Set aside due to tight vendor lock-in, differing payload schemas, and rapid API churn.
  • Heavy agentic orchestration frameworks (e.g., LangChain core): Set aside due to opinionated abstractions, large dependency graphs, and frequent breaking interface changes.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Sync/Async Execution: Client contract provides parallel asynchronous coroutine hooks alongside blocking execution primitives.
  • Recorded Replay (VCR Engine): Captures sanitized production completions during staging smoke tests to regenerate CI fixtures deterministically.
  • Resilience Multi-Gateway: Active-passive routing that shifts downstream provider targets upon encountering HTTP 429 (Rate Limit) or 5xx exceptions.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Eliminates CI pipeline flakiness and network dependency; enables multi-provider failover in production.
  • Performance & Latency: Client translation overhead is under 2ms; mock client execution completes in sub-millisecond durations.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Guarantees zero unnecessary inference spend in automated pipelines; simplifies provider price-performance switching.
  • Operability: Standardizes metrics (token usage, latency, error taxonomy) and distributed tracing across all model interactions.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Leaky Vendor Context: Allowing vendor-specific parameters (e.g., custom top-k or system prompt formatting) to pass unfiltered through the domain interface.
  • Network Calls in CI: Running unit or integration tests that require live API keys or reach external LLM endpoints.
  • Unchecked Mock Drift: Mock fixtures remaining static while upstream model formats evolve; mitigated by regular recorded replay updates.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
1. Define LLMClient base interface in domain core.
  2. Implement MockLLMClient with deterministic response mapping and inject it into existing test harnesses.
  3. Integrate LiteLLMClient in runtime bootstrapping, passing provider credentials via configuration management.
  4. Transition all agent consumers to receive the interface via dependency injection.

docs.title: Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Provider-Agnostic LLM Facade abstracts upstream Large Language Model (LLM) vendor APIs behind a consistent, unified programmatic interface. It decouples core agentic orchestrators, prompt engines, and workflow pipelines from proprietary SDK specifications, error models, and payload representations.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• Multi-provider environments requiring dynamic model routing, failover, or runtime load distribution across vendors (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Ollama).
  • Systems requiring deterministic, zero-cost offline integration testing and CI validation via mock implementations with contract parity.
  • Architectures seeking insulation against upstream breaking API changes, token schema alterations, and vendor lock-in.
  • Enterprise environments mandating standardized observability, cost allocation, token metering, and centralized governance hooks.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• Trivial single-model scripts or proofs-of-concept where the abstraction introduces unnecessary indirection overhead.
  • Specialized systems requiring hyper-specific, vendor-proprietary features that lack standard cross-provider abstractions (e.g., vendor-specific fine-tuning endpoints or proprietary real-time stateful streaming APIs) unless strictly isolated as vendor-specific extensions.
  • Edge environments with extreme binary size or dependency constraints unable to sustain wrapper dependencies.

docs.text:
• LLM Client Interface & Base Abstraction (src/cas_runner/llm/base.py): Defines the core invocation protocol, structured response contracts, standardized exception hierarchy, and common configuration parameters across all implementations.
  • LiteLLM Client Adapter (src/cas_runner/llm/litellm_client.py): Implements the unified interface by wrapping LiteLLM, translating normalized prompts into vendor-specific HTTP payloads, and harmonizing disparate response formats and token usage telemetry.
  • Mock LLM Client (src/cas_runner/llm/mock_client.py): Provides predictable, fixture-driven mock completions and structured output parsing for unit tests, offline continuous integration, and synthetic failure injections.
  • Agent Execution Pipeline (src/cas_runner/runner.py): Consumes the LLM Client Facade polymorphically during agent workflow tasks without awareness of the underlying model endpoint or execution environment.

docs.title: Recommended Choices
docs.text:
• Unified Engine: LiteLLM was selected as the underlying transport and translation layer due to its lightweight profile, active maintenance, broad model coverage (100+ LLMs), and native support for OpenAI-compatible schema bridging.
  • Interface Definition: Python typing.Protocol and pydantic.BaseModel for compile-time contract verification and runtime schema validation of structured completions.
  • Mock Driver: In-memory deterministic rule engine providing canned completion schemas and regex-based response fixtures.

docs.title: Alternatives Set Aside
docs.text:
• Direct Vendor SDKs (e.g., openai, anthropic): Rejected due to high vendor lock-in, divergent error paradigms, and high maintenance costs when switching or cascading models.
  • Heavyweight Frameworks (e.g., LangChain / LlamaIndex): Rejected for low-level execution pipelines due to excessive dependency footprints, breaking API churn, and opacity around prompt mutations.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Execution: Supports synchronous blocking execution for batch CLI workflows alongside asyncio-native interfaces for high-concurrency streaming agent services.
  • Multi-Provider Fallback Circuit: A cascading variant where requests automatically fail over from primary cloud models to secondary models or on-premise Ollama instances upon encountering rate limits (HTTP 429) or outages (HTTP 5xx).
  • Dual Production/Mock Mode: Automated dependency injection variant switching dynamically between LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient based on runtime configuration (LLM_ENV=test vs LLM_ENV=production).

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Normalizes error handling by mapping diverse vendor HTTP error codes into canonical exceptions (RateLimitExceeded, ModelUnavailable, ContextWindowExceeded, InvalidRequestException), facilitating deterministic automated retry policies.
  • Performance & Latency: Implements native request pass-through with minimal Python wrapping overhead (<2ms latency tax). Supports connection pooling, persistent keep-alive sessions, and streaming responses to minimize time-to-first-token (TTFT).
  • Cost & Efficiency: Enforces centralized tracking of prompt and completion token counts per tenant or workflow step. Enables automated routing of lightweight tasks to cost-effective models without application code refactoring.
  • Operability: Emits OpenTelemetry-compliant metrics, standard structured logs (model identifier, token counts, execution latency), and explicit audit trails across all provider invocations.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Vendor-Specific Leakage: Passing vendor-unique request parameters directly through application prompts or business logic rather than standardizing them within facade config classes. Remedy: Encapsulate vendor flags within strongly-typed adapter configurations.
  • Untyped Generic Payloads: Exposing raw string responses without structured parsing or JSON schema enforcement, resulting in fragile downstream parsing. Remedy: Standardize on Pydantic-based structured response contracts.
  • Direct Instantiation: Hardcoding LiteLLMClient() directly inside agent steps instead of injecting the base interface. Remedy: Enforce dependency injection or factory patterns across runner components.
  • Unmocked Testing: Running test suites directly against paid provider APIs, causing pipeline flakiness and high costs. Remedy: Gate live API tests behind explicit integration flags and mandate MockLLMClient for continuous integration.

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
1. Establish the Contract: Define the abstract base client protocol and standardized response models in a shared package.
  2. Implement Facade Wrapper: Wrap current direct vendor client calls into LiteLLMClient, mapping existing configurations to standard settings.
  3. Deploy Mock Implementation: Implement and adopt MockLLMClient across the CI test suite to eliminate reliance on external API keys during pipeline runs.
  4. Refactor Invocations: Refactor agent runners and governance evaluators to consume the facade via dependency injection.

docs.title: Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Provider-Agnostic LLM Gateway encapsulates model invocations behind a unified interface, decoupling application and agentic logic from vendor-specific APIs. It allows seamless switching between multi-cloud LLM providers and enables zero-cost deterministic offline execution via local mock implementations.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When applications or autonomous agents need multi-provider routing (e.g., fallback between OpenAI, Anthropic, or local models) without refactoring business logic.
  • When automated continuous integration (CI) test suites and local developer environments need to run deterministic evaluation loops without external network dependencies, latency, or API token expenses.
  • When governance policies mandate centralized telemetry, rate limiting, token usage tracking, and schema validation across heterogeneous LLM calls.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• Single-model, low-complexity prototypes or scripts where direct SDK integration introduces negligible architectural lock-in.
  • Ultra-low latency streaming use cases requiring proprietary protocol optimizations (e.g., raw WebSockets directly into custom on-premise hardware) where an abstraction layer introduces unacceptable overhead.
  • Scenarios where application logic relies heavily on deep, non-standardized provider-proprietary features that cannot be normalized across an industry interface without extensive leaky abstractions.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• LLM Gateway Interface (src/cas_runner/llm/base.py): Exposes an abstract client contract (e.g., unified generate, embed, and structured output methods) defining strict input and output schemas regardless of the backing model.
  • LiteLLM Client Adapter (src/cas_runner/llm/litellm_client.py): Translates standard gateway requests into provider-specific schemas (e.g., Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock), managing authentication, backoff retries, and dynamic model routing.
  • Mock Client Adapter (src/cas_runner/llm/mock_client.py): Delivers configurable, deterministic synthetic responses and recorded fixtures to support hermetic unit testing, CI pipelines, and zero-cost local development.
  • Prompt & Schema Validator (src/cas_runner/llm/validators.py): Validates structured responses against Pydantic or JSON schemas prior to returning outputs to the caller, abstracting schema repair logic.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text:
Recommended Primary Adapter: LiteLLM or an internal unified wrapper over standard REST/gRPC endpoints. LiteLLM is selected for its broad multi-provider coverage (100+ models), built-in fallback routing, and transparent translation of standard OpenAI-compatible payloads.

Alternatives Considered and Set Aside: - Direct Vendor SDKs (e.g., openai, anthropic): Set aside due to strong vendor lock-in, disparate error handling semantics, and inability to run deterministic test fixtures without deep monkey-patching. - LangChain / LlamaIndex core bindings: Set aside when only standard LLM calling is required; direct gateway abstractions avoid heavy framework dependencies and frequent upstream breaking changes.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
• Offline Mock Variant: Directs all LLM calls to in-memory fixtures or recorded disk caches, guaranteeing reproducible evaluation runs and zero credential requirements in CI.
  • Resilient Multi-Provider Fallback: Configures the adapter to automatically retry transient network errors or rate limit failures against secondary backup providers (e.g., fallback from primary Claude 3.5 Sonnet to GPT-4o).
  • Self-Hosted / On-Premise Gateway: Routes calls through a self-hosted API gateway instance (e.g., LiteLLM Proxy or vLLM) for enterprise telemetry enforcement and egress IP whitelisting.

docs.title: Non-functional characteristics
docs.text:
• Reliability: Mitigates downstream provider outages via automated failover and backoff strategies; isolates business logic from upstream API deprecations.
  • Performance & Latency: Adds minimal overhead (<2ms in-memory translation latency); supports asynchronous streaming and optional prompt/response response caching to minimize roundtrips.
  • Cost & Efficiency: Drastically cuts development and automated testing expenses by routing CI workflows through the Mock Client Adapter; enables cross-provider cost optimization based on task complexity.
  • Operability: Unifies logging, audit tracking, token counting, and metrics instrumentation into a single chokepoint.

docs.title: Anti-patterns & known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Leaky Vendor Features: Exposing provider-specific hyper-parameters or system prompt formats directly through the gateway contract, breaking consumer interchangeability. (Remedy: Normalize request options or use an explicit typed metadata map).
  • Mock Drift: Allowing the Mock Client Adapter schemas to drift out of sync with actual production provider schemas. (Remedy: Maintain periodic contract testing suites validating real provider responses against mock contract assertions).
  • Silent Schema Coercion Failures: Swallowing schema parsing errors from unpredictable LLM outputs. (Remedy: Implement strict validation with explicit retry loops and repair prompts at the gateway level).

docs.title: Adoption guidance
docs.text:
1. Identify all direct model SDK imports across the project and define a common abstract base class (BaseLLMClient) capturing current input/output contracts.
  2. Implement the MockLLMClient adapter and migrate automated unit and integration tests to verify deterministic execution without API keys.
  3. Implement the LiteLLMClient adapter for production environments, wrapping environment-based provider selection.
  4. Route all agent orchestration components through the gateway factory.

docs.title: Reference Architecture: Pure Functional Health Evaluation
Reference Architecture: Pure Functional Health Evaluation
Purpose & when to use this
docs.text: The Pure Functional Health Evaluation pattern establishes a decoupled, deterministic mechanism for assessing system, governance, and operational health. By structuring health and risk logic as pure functions that operate strictly on passed metrics snapshots, systems ensure identical evaluations across reporting dashboards, background monitors, and validation pipelines without mutable state dependencies.

docs.title: When to use this
docs.text:
• When computing health indicators, compliance scores, or operational readiness across dashboards and monitoring monitors.
  • When business evaluation logic must be verified across multiple environments without needing database connections, mocks, or network I/O.
  • When evaluations must be run concurrently, repeatedly, or on transient client data without mutating underlying system entities.
  • When health diagnostics require human-readable explanation strings derived deterministically from the same state vector.

docs.title: When NOT to use this
docs.text:
• When evaluation rules inherently depend on direct streaming state changes or dynamic database cursors that cannot be pre-fetched into a snapshot.
  • When status calculation requires immediate asynchronous external consensus (e.g., quorum polling) during the calculation phase.
  • In trivial single-field threshold checks where an embedded boolean flag suffices and explicit domain modeling introduces unnecessary boilerplate.

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    consumer["Dashboard / Consumer Service (Container)"]
    collector["Metrics Collector / Fetcher (Container)"]
    evaluator["Pure Health Evaluator (Domain Function)"]
    statusEnum["HealthStatus & Reasons (Domain Value Model)"]
    metricsStore[("Metrics Store (Data store)")]

    consumer -->|1. Request Health Assessment| collector
    collector -->|2. Fetch Metrics Snapshot| metricsStore
    collector -->|3. Pass Immutable Metrics| evaluator
    evaluator -->|4. Return HealthStatus + Reasons| statusEnum
    statusEnum -->|5. Render Deterministic View| consumer

    classDef store fill:#1168bd,stroke:#0b4884,color:#fff
    classDef external fill:#666666,stroke:#333333,color:#fff
